Here 's Why That 's Missing the Point <p> The U.S. government is considering a " Manhattan Project-style initiative " for artificial intelligence development without realising that , unlike nuclear power , AI does n't have an end-point writes Satyen K. Bordoloi . <p> When J. Robert Oppenheimer recruited physicists for the Manhattan Project , he gave them a well-defined goal : to build an atomic bomb using uranium and plutonium . The project concluded with the development , testing , and deployment of ' Little Boy ' and ' Fat Man , ' which left profound and lasting impacts on the world 's psyche . Now , the U.S. is proposing a similar initiative for AI , driven by concerns about Chinese technological advancements . <p> The Proposal : In November , the bipartisan U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission ( USCC ) released a report , in which the first suggestion was that : " Congress establish and fund a Manhattan Project-like program dedicated to racing to and acquiring an Artificial General Intelligence ( AGI ) capability . " This proposal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the first atomic bombs , but it stems from a fundamental misunderstanding of both AI development and the historical context of the Manhattan Project . <p> AI researchers and developers working on various AI projects , illustrating the diverse and decentralised nature of AI development ( Image : lexica.art ) <p> The Original Blueprint : The Manhattan Project succeeded because it brought together the US 's brightest minds , unlimited resources , and a single , unambiguous goal . Scientists aimed to achieve a nuclear chain reaction to release unprecedented energy . They could test their progress , measure their results , and determine when they would likely reach their goal . The project had clear scientific objectives , measurable milestones , a definite endpoint , known scientific principles , and a binary outcome -- it would either work or it would n't . <p> The AI Dilemma : In contrast , AI development , especially the pursuit of AGI , is more of a moving target than a fixed goal . AGI is often described as AI systems that match or exceed human intelligence , but there is no @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it the ability to pass tests , create art , solve complex problems , or understand nuanced emotions ? Current generative AI systems like ChatGPT , Gemini , and LLaMA have achieved some of these goals , but we are far from achieving true AGI . <p> In a Reuters report , USCC Commissioner Jacob Helberg stated , " China is racing towards AGI ... ( AP ) <p> Summary <p> US President Donald Trump may have nominated Kevin Warsh to head the US Federal Reserve for his views on easing credit , but his assumptions could be flawed . Warsh could be in for a reality check . <p> Now that Kevin Warsh has been nominated as the next chair of the US Federal Reserve Board , it is worth asking how different a Warsh Fed would be from the current one . Aside from the need to calm markets spooked by his attacks on Fed independence , one reason may be that Warsh believes that AI and other technological innovations will reduce inflation and thus allow for lower policy rates . <p> But there is a problem here : If AI reduces inflation , it would do so through higher GDP and productivity growth , implying the need for a higher equilibrium inflation-adjusted policy rate and real long-term rate , even if lower inflation implies a potentially lower nominal policy rate . But there could be a problem here , too . With Trump-appointee Michelle Bowman now @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ probably accelerate efforts to ease credit conditions even at the risk of fuelling credit and asset bubbles . And that , in turn , could undermine financial stability at a time when markets are already frothy , leverage is high and private credit is wobbling . <p> Warsh argues that unwinding the Fed 's balance sheet will allow it to reduce policy rates more sharply on the logic that quantitative tightening ( QT ) causes financial conditions to tighten . But he is wrong about this . <p> Under the post-2008 regime , interest rates on excess reserves paid to banks nullify the impact of those reserves on credit creation and financial conditions . That is why the Fed has been able to reduce its balance sheet by 25% without triggering tighter financial conditions . There is no reason to think that more QT will justify much lower policy rates . <p> Warsh 's opposition to the current ample-reserves regime may come back to bite him . If Warsh truly wants to avoid new emergency QE episodes , he should favour rather than oppose ample excess reserves . <p> Moreover , Warsh has suggested that he may support a new Fed-Treasury accord in which monetary policy would be further removed from fiscal policy and public-debt management . For example , this could mean reducing the Fed 's balance sheet and buying short-term public debt rather than long-term bonds , as was the case before the 2008-09 financial crisis . <p> But putting aside the fact that this could also phase out the current ample-reserves regime , further reducing the Fed 's holdings of long-term bonds would force the Treasury to double down on its Activist Treasury Issuance ( ATI ) policy , implying that there would be even more manipulation of the market for long-term debt and mortgage-backed securities . <p> A new Fed-Treasury accord could lead to even more backdoor ATI and more mixing of monetary and fiscal policy , the exact opposite of the arrangement 's stated goal . These are real risks . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ' into issues such as financial stability , climate change and inequality . @@135269981 <p> Residents of a small Kerala town rejected a state-led development blueprint they feared would destroy farms , water systems and livelihoods . <p> Instead of going to court , the municipality spent nearly three years creating a participatory " People 's Plan " with planners , volunteers and hundreds of residents . <p> The new master plan prioritises pedestrian mobility , climate resilience and the protection of historic water systems and urban commons . <p> On October 18 , 2021 , residents of Chittur-Thathamangalam , a small town in Kerala 's Palakkad district , received something the town had never had before in its 125-year history : a Master Plan . <p> The Draft Master Plan 2031 , prepared by the state 's town planning department , outlined an ambitious vision for the town 's future . It proposed a wide range of infrastructure projects , including extensive road widening , four bypasses and ring roads , two lorry terminals , a new bus stand , and a terminal market , among 85 development initiatives intended to spur economic growth . <p> But when the town 's newly elected @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ roughly 32,000 residents examined the proposals closely , many were alarmed . <p> They concluded that , if actualised , the infrastructure projects proposed under the Draft Master Plan 's " pro-growth " paradigm could fundamentally reshape the character of their town . Local representatives argued that theseproposals would wipe out nearly 80 per cent of the town 's retail economy , while also requiring the demolition of hundreds of homes , community buildings and acres of agricultural fields . <p> Residents warned that such development would inevitably lead to flooding , drought , unemployment , and displacement . They feared that any intervention altering their existing landscape -- nearly half of which is under agriculture , mainly paddy , banana , and coconut cultivation , along with locally managed irrigation systems that shape water flows , ecology , and the commons -- would jeopardise their future . <p> So instead of accepting the state 's blueprint , the town decided to challenge it . <h> An alternative vision <p> Faced with widespread opposition from residents , including associations of traders , merchants and paddy farmers , the municipality chose @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Master Plan 2031 , it began work on its own alternative -- a participatory planning process that would ultimately produce the Chittur-Thathamangalam Master Plan 2042 . <p> Over the next 33 months , the municipality worked with planners , volunteers , local residents and academic experts to create what supporters say is India 's first municipality-led participatory master plan aimed at protecting shared community resources while preparing for climate change . <p> The initiative drew on provisions in the Kerala Town and Country Planning ( KTCP ) Act 2016 , which mandates public participation during the preparation of master plans . <p> To guide the process , the municipality appointed a two-member Master Plan Expert Committee ( MPEC ) , consisting of urban planners Jayaraj Sundaresan and Malini Krishnankutty . <p> Rather than taking the draft plan to court , the committee decided to focus on building a locally grounded alternative . <p> " We believed that the best way to counter the draft plan was to develop a better one , " says Sundaresan , who is originally from Chittur-Thathamangalam . <h> Rediscovering the ancient water system <p> One @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ plan , planners say , was the town 's centuries-old water management system . <p> According to Sundaresan , the town contains a remarkable network of 171 human-made ponds -- known locally as kulams . The heritage water management system is connected by canals and natural streams flowing through cascading paddy fields . <p> Together with the Sokanasini river , these features form an integrated drainage and irrigation system that enable water harvesting and more , typical of many historic settlements in South India . " These water-channelling systems have evolved over roughly 1,500 years , " Sundaresan explains . " They support groundwater percolation , agriculture , livestock , drinking water supply and flood mitigation . They act as the ecological foundation of human settlements . " <p> Yet the Draft Master Plan 2031 did not recognise this network . <p> The planners also found that other shared spaces -- including a yarn-stretching ground used by the town 's textile weaver community and a temple festival ground -- had been classified simply as vacant land and proposed for redevelopment as parks . <p> The old plan classified a yarn-stretching @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ vacant land.Jayaraj Sundaresan <p> For Krishnankutty , these omissions highlight a deeper problem with conventional urban planning methods . Existing Land Use ( ELU ) maps , she says , typically rely on broad categories such as residential , commercial or industrial land use . While useful in large cities , such classifications often fail to capture the complex and overlapping ways in which land is used in smaller towns . <p> " In reality , the same piece of land can support multiple activities and it is important to record all of them , " Krishnankutty says . " Paddy fields , for instance , may also be used seasonally by pastoral duck owners whose flocks fertilise the fields . " <p> Understanding these layered relationships between people and land , she argues , requires planners to document all practices using terms from the local language and create appropriate terms for categories . " In India , a large number of people live in informal housing and rely on informal livelihoods , " she says . " Very often , it is the so-called ' unplanned ' commons -- @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " <p> Krishnankutty says it is imperative to move away from modernist planning approaches that prioritise protecting property rights and acknowledge the long tradition of treating land and water as shared resources . " Historically , both land and water were viewed as commons , to be used judiciously in the larger public interest . Across India 's older settlements , diverse systems of water management exist -- from qanats and eries to khazans and many others . These traditions and practices must be integrated into our planning , " she says . <h> Building a plan together <p> The effort to develop the People 's Plan relied heavily on volunteer work and local cooperation , establishing the mandatory special committee to invite and review suggestions and objections on the Draft Master Plan . @@135269996 <p> The future of housing raises some serious environmental concerns . Construction has been linked to 39 per cent of global carbon emissions , and the concrete industry alone is responsible for 8 per cent of the world 's greenhouse gases . <p> Solutions will be especially useful in Africa , because so much building still needs to be done . The continent 's population is projected to grow from around 1.5 billion to an estimated 2.4 billion people by 2050 . There 's already a housing backlog of 50 million homes . <p> Green housing could be one of the solutions . Green homes are built using less energy and water , and with natural and often recycled resources . They are designed to use less water and power , and emit lower levels of greenhouse gases . <p> As sustainable housing researchers , we have extensively investigated the evolution of green housing . We 've looked at how green homes are certified , and what kinds of policies support them . We 've also investigated the barriers to financing green homes and looked into what 's preventing a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and construction . <p> Our latest research set out to map how green housing developments are financed around the world . <p> We reviewed all global studies on green housing finance over a 20 year period ( 2003-2023 ) . Our aim was to uncover the main financial instruments used by private green housing developers , and how these types of finance support sustainability in the construction sector . <p> Our research found that green housing finance products must address developmental targets , sustainability , cost , water and energy efficiency , materials , and climate change risk . <p> Sustainability concerns are rising globally . Home owners and developers have a role to play in the adoption of environmentally friendly building practices . Knowing more about green housing finance empowers housing stakeholders to go green . <p> Development finance institutions and commercial banks need to work more closely together to offer practical green housing loans . They also need to make sure that developers and individual home builders know about the benefits of and choices they have for going green . <h> The development finance gap <p> Green buildings @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ efficient use of resources . They also reduce the carbon footprint created by environmentally unfriendly building materials like concrete . They stimulate local economies and small enterprises by driving new technology , specialised skills , and the use of locally sourced materials . <p> Countries in Africa want to mitigate climate change , adapt to it , reduce the cost of energy , and manage their dwindling resources , such as water . One way to achieve this is to make new housing projects more water and energy efficient . Climate finance is a significant way of funding green housing . <p> However , the financial tools that make this possible are limited and not accessible to all people . In Africa , as seen in Nigeria , South Africa , Kenya and Ghana , economically and ecologically viable cities seem out of reach . Green homes potentially reduce electricity and water bills over time . But their higher upfront costs make them unaffordable for most people in these countries . Green homes can seem like a luxury rather than a necessity . <p> Very few green housing financing opportunities @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ roadblock . These councils can collaborate across countries , exchange knowledge and make sure that all countries in Africa have access to the same information about sustainable housing practices , expertise and materials . <p> Green building certification bodies must adopt and standardise local approaches to environmental sustainability . @@135270235 <h> Wildlife relocation is rare in India , often riddled with state pride issues such as in Gir or treated as a last resort . As home deliveries surge , gig workers inhale toxic traffic fumes for hours , and an Atmospheric Pollution Research study ( 2023 ) shows they face elevated exposure to particulate matter and volatile organic compounds , revealing the unequal health costs of urban convenience . There is a need to declare war on pollution and commit to sustained , enforceable methods to address this " airpocalypse " . But new research shows that , when it comes to environmental conservation , the picture is more complicated . <p> Using granular satellite data on forest cover , my co-authors and I sought to understand whether electing women to state legislatures leads to improvements in their constituencies and whether any gains persist throughout their electoral terms . This interpretation is consistent with earlier research showing that legislators ' overlapping social identities often shape policy priorities and public-goods provision in India . <p> India has been actively working to increase women 's political representation , including through a constitutional amendment reserving 33% of seats in the lower house of parliament , state assemblies , and Delhi Legislative Assembly for women . About 43% of IMF loan programs in 100 countries from 1980 to 2014 , for instance , targeted food and agriculture -- of which more than 59% of conditionalities involved the abolition or reduction of state support and promotion of unregulated market forces . @@135282502 <h> After Bel ? m : Rebuilding Human Security in a Warming World <p> In my earlier reflections ahead of COP30 , I emphasized the moral urgency of climate action . Bel ? m revealed something even more fundamental : the structural urgency . The gathering in November 2025 , held in the heart of the Amazon , did more than host another climate conference . It exposed the world 's readiness -- and unreadiness -- for the climate era . In a region where rivers , forests , and communities form a single living system , the discussions made clear that climate change is not only transforming ecosystems ; it is eroding the systems that protect human life . The question after Bel ? m is no longer whether action is necessary , but whether our institutions can shield people from what is already unfolding . <p> The Climate Era Is a Human Security Era <p> For decades , climate diplomacy revolved around emissions targets and negotiation texts . Yet the conversations that resonated most strongly in Bel ? m were not about carbon metrics alone . They were @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and the stability of societies . Climate change has moved from the margins of environmental policy to the center of human survival . In effect , the climate era has become the era of human security . <p> From a medical perspective , this shift is already visible . Heatwaves have become mass-casualty events . Emergency departments fill with patients suffering dehydration and cardiovascular stress . Floods destroy clinics and hospitals as quickly as they devastate homes . Drought reshapes nutrition , spreads disease , and deepens psychological distress . Displacement fractures families and weakens the social networks on which health depends . These are not distant projections ; they are present-day emergencies . Frontline communities have understood this for years . Bel ? m made their reality impossible to ignore . <p> Every disaster now underscores that human security is inseparable from climate security . <p> Our Protective Systems Are Failing Faster Than We Are Repairing Them <p> One of the clearest lessons from Bel ? m was the widening gap between global ambition and local resilience . Governments presented plans for mitigation and adaptation , yet many @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ strain . <p> * Aging infrastructure -- from water networks to transport and energy systems -- was designed for a climate that no longer exists . Under stronger storms , wildfires , and rising seas , these systems are increasingly failing . <p> Climate-related disasters have increased dramatically in recent decades , yet institutional adaptation has moved far more slowly . The result is a dangerous imbalance : climate impacts are accelerating faster than the systems designed to protect society . <p> The Amazon 's Lesson : Ecosystems Are Public Health Infrastructure <p> Holding COP30 in Bel ? m was more than symbolic ; it was diagnostic . The Amazon functions as a planetary life-support system . Its forests regulate rainfall across continents , stabilize temperatures , and sustain biodiversity that underpins medicine , food systems , and disease control . When the Amazon weakens , the consequences extend directly to human health and stability . <p> Indigenous communities reminded the world that protecting ecosystems is not an environmental luxury but a public health necessity . Their knowledge and stewardship represent one of humanity 's most effective forms of climate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ recognize their rights and leadership . <p> What Bel ? m Did Not Resolve <p> Despite progress in climate finance and ecosystem protection , important gaps remain . Climate displacement still lacks a clear international legal framework . Mental health impacts -- from ecological anxiety to disaster trauma -- remain largely overlooked . Persons with disabilities continue to be excluded from many adaptation strategies and emergency plans . And the relationship between climate stress and conflict remains insufficiently addressed , even as environmental pressures increasingly intersect with political instability . These omissions leave millions unprotected . <p> Toward a New Global Human Security Compact <p> Bel ? m should mark the beginning of a new phase in climate governance -- one focused not only on reducing emissions but on strengthening the systems that safeguard life . This requires resilient health systems capable of withstanding climate shocks ; inclusive adaptation strategies that protect women , children , Indigenous peoples , and persons with disabilities ; early-warning systems grounded in science and community participation ; and infrastructure designed for future climate realities rather than past patterns . <p> Equally important is transparent @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ including artificial intelligence , must be used ethically -- to improve monitoring , prediction , and resilience rather than expand surveillance or militarization . <p> Human security must become the organizing principle of climate action . Bel ? m reminded the world that protecting the planet is inseparable from protecting people . @@135282504 <h> Sunlight travels 93 million miles to reach the earth , None of them through the Strait of Hormuz <p> A week ago I made my geopolitical point about the then-new Iran war -- any leader with a brain would be trying to build up their clean energy capacity to avoid the kind of fossil fuel squeeze now underway . The message has spread ( eloquent explanation from the venerable Paul Krugman this morning ) . <p> But since this is a teachable moment like few others , I wanted to in a sense make the same point again , but this time in a way that I hope is useful to all of you as you try to explain the possible futures to friends , neighbors , and perfect strangers . I think it 's an exercise perhaps worth copying and pasting , because it highlights something important : the incredible simplicity of clean energy , as compared to the Rube Goldberg contraption that is fossil fuel . <p> We 're very used to the fossil fuel paradigm , and so it does n't strike us as complicated . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ gas for your car , someone first needs to have drilled for oil -- in a few places ( Saudi Arabia ) this is still relatively easy , but increasingly it means figuring out how to go a mile beneath the surface of the sea , or frack the subsurface geology , which is to say blow it apart . Once you 've collected your crude , you need to carry it to a port , often through a pipeline that must cross mountain and desert , and there load it on to a giant ship , which must sail the seas . Upon arrival somewhere , it needs to be piped to a refinery , which is among the most complicated pieces of machinery known to man . There it must be separated by heating in a distillation column , so that the light products -- gasoline -- rise to the top , and heavy products -- say , asphalt -- sink to the bottom . You use heat and pressure and chemical catalysts to " crack " some of the heavier molecules into lighter , more valuable products @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ remove impurities like sulfur . You pipe it part of the way to its final destination , and load it into trucks for delivery to gas stations , where it is stored in underground tanks , until someone appears with a credit card to pump it into his vehicle . In the engine of the car it is mixed with air inside a cylinder and compressed ; a spark plug fires , forcing a piston to move ; this linear motion is converted by a crankshaft into rotational energy to move the car ; meanwhile the piston pushes out the burned gases . <p> This " works " -- the proof is all around us , in a society built for cars . But man is it inelegant . Think of all the things that can go wrong . Your oil well can leak , coating the surrounding water with oil ; if you 're fracking , you can trigger earthquakes . The pipeline can leak too -- and they do so fairly routinely , coating waterways or farm fields with crude . Your ship might run aground and spill @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ oh I do n't know an ill-advised regime change war because it must travel through a narrow strait . Refineries can catch on fire -- in wartime because they become easy targets for your enemy . The underground storage tank at the gas station can leak too , often polluting groundwater . And the engine where you 're burning this gas can break , because the drivetrain -- depending on how you count -- has hundreds of thousands of moving parts . ( A crankshaft , say , typically rides on five main bearings , each with two bearing shells ) . <p> And even when they work perfectly , internal combustion engines waste enormous amounts of that gasoline -- only about 25 percent of its energy actually moves the car , with the rest spent on heat , friction , and idling . And when you burn that gas , you produce a fair amount of pollution . The quantities of carbon monoxide and particulates can be reduced fairly dramatically with good pollution control equipment , like a catalytic converter that needs some platinum or palladium or rhodium . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ carbon dioxide per gallon of gasoline burned -- indeed , if you make the engine " cleaner , " it actually produces slightly more co2 . How much carbon dioxide ? A gallon of gasoline weighs about six pounds . When you burn it , the carbon atoms mix with oxygen atoms in the air to form about 19 pounds of carbon dioxide . The average American car driven the average American distance releases about its own weight in co2 each year . And that is why the polar ice caps are melting . That is why we just had the second-warmest winter in American history . That is why hundreds of millions of people have to flee their homes . <p> Now think about an EV instead . The sun produces energy by fusing hydrogen atoms into helium . It travels 93 million miles in about eight minutes and 20 seconds ( seven seconds more when our orbit takes us furthest away ) . Those photons then strike the silicon atoms in a photovoltaic panel , knocking loose electrons that produce a stream of direct current electricity ; an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that to AC power , which can be pumped directly into the battery of an EV where the motor uses electromagnetism to create a rotating magnetic field in a stator , which spins the inner rotor to propel the car . There are about 20 moving parts in the engine , and it is 80 to 90 percent efficient . There is no exhaust and almost no noise . That 's it . And if you poured those electrons into an e-bike instead of an EV , it 's even better : a penny 's worth of power is good for three miles or so.The same principles apply to electric buses , electric ferries , and so on . <p> This method cuts maintenance and operation costs in half for drivers , and the EV is at this point not much more expensive than the average car ( in China and most of the rest of the world , it 's less ) . More to the point , it produces no pollution -- this would reduce global health costs by a trillion dollars a year or so . And @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ expected to cost the planet $38 trillion annually by mid-century . Those numbers represent millions upon millions of people who would get to live instead of die . <p> Also , no one can use a missile to shoot down a photon in mid-air . It is essentially war-proof . <p> Also , you can do it on your roof or your balcony , or in your community . You do n't require an oligarch . It would impoverish Vladimir Putin , Mohammed bin Salman , the CEO of Exxon . ( And that 's why we do n't work harder to get it done ; they 're in the way ) . <p> For a long time we could n't do this . The solar cell was n't invented until 1954 , and for decades it produced very expensive power . But now , thanks to activists and engineers , it produces the cheapest power on planet earth . <p> In a sane world we would be spending all our time and money building solar panels just as fast as we could . @@135282506 <h> No Climate Justice Without Disability Inclusion <p> The formal recognition of the Disability Caucus within the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change ( UNFCCC ) is more than an institutional adjustment . It is a decisive step toward inclusive climate governance -- one that reframes climate justice through human rights , lived experience , and structural accountability . <p> For the first time , persons with disabilities and their representative organizations have an acknowledged platform within the multilateral process that shapes global mitigation targets , adaptation strategies , and climate finance flows under the Paris Agreement . Their presence signals a shift from consultation at the margins to participation within the architecture of decision-making itself . <p> Yet this milestone is not about procedural access alone . It is about people . <p> When floods sweep through low-lying communities , when wildfires force sudden evacuation , when heatwaves strain fragile health systems , persons with disabilities are often among the first to experience the consequences -- and the last to be systematically considered in planning . Climate policy that does not account for human diversity risks reinforcing the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Structural Intersection of Climate Risk <p> Disaster-risk evidence consistently shows disproportionate exposure among persons with disabilities during climate-related emergencies . Barriers to accessible information , evacuation routes designed without mobility considerations , and interruptions in medical or assistive services can transform a hazard into a life-threatening crisis . <p> Consider the reality of an individual who depends on a ventilator during prolonged power outages , or a deaf resident who receives no accessible early-warning message before a storm surge . These are not hypothetical vulnerabilities ; they are predictable consequences of systems designed without inclusion at their core . <p> The aftermath of the 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami demonstrated how accessibility reforms and community-based planning can strengthen resilience . Inclusive design does not weaken efficiency ; it enhances it . When infrastructure , communication systems , and emergency protocols are built to accommodate diverse needs , entire communities benefit . <p> In regions of the Global South -- where climate exposure intersects with fragile infrastructure and limited public services -- the stakes are even higher . There , disability inclusion is inseparable from development equity . <p> A @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Caucus aligns directly with obligations under the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities ( CRPD ) , particularly : <p> This is the essence of inclusive climate governance : not parallel tracks of environmental ambition and social justice , but a unified framework in which legitimacy depends on participation and accessibility . <p> In practical terms , this may mean ensuring evacuation centers are accessible before the next cyclone season , mandating inclusive renewable-energy installations , or conditioning funding approval on accessibility compliance . Such measures translate recognition into accountability . <p> From Advocacy to Institutional Legitimacy <p> This formal recognition , announced by the International Disability Alliance on 27 February 2026 , represents the culmination of nearly a decade of coordinated global advocacy . <p> Since the 2015 United Nations Climate Change Conference , disability organizations have worked steadily to build a coordinated global coalition . @@135282512 <h> A Spring Too Soon : Kashmir 's Altered February <p> Kashmir has always experienced time in ways that seem to rise above dates and calendars . In the Valley , seasons are sensed through the temperament of mountains , the whisper of rivers , and the steady assurance of nature 's recurring cycles . February has traditionally carried the weight of lingering winter -- icy dawns , snow-laden rooftops , and the quiet comfort of kangris glowing beneath heavy pherans . It has long symbolized endurance , bridging the piercing severity of Chillai Kalan with the tentative promise of spring . This year , however , February felt altered , as though the cadence of time itself had subtly shifted . <p> Meteorological evidence shows this shift was not imagined . Monitoring stations across Kashmir recorded temperatures 9-11 ? C above normal , with Srinagar nearing 20-21 ? C , among its highest February readings on record . Gulmarg crossed earlier benchmarks , while Qazigund and Kokernag also experienced unusual warmth . These are not random variations but signs of a broader climatic trend reshaping the Valley 's seasonal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ clothing , bright afternoons , early blossoms , it carries deeper concern . In Kashmir , winter is more than a season ; it is a vital ecological reserve . Mountain snow acts as natural water storage , slowly feeding rivers , springs , and irrigation systems in warmer months . When winter weakens , this delicate hydrological balance begins to strain . <p> This year 's elevated temperatures coincided with extended dryness and reduced precipitation . Observations reveal significant deficits in both snowfall and rainfall , while forecasts have repeatedly indicated prolonged dry spells . Such conditions accelerate snowmelt , limit groundwater recharge , and cause an earlier reduction in stream flows . The Jhelum River and its tributaries , essential lifelines of the Valley , already exhibit subtle but worrying signs of strain . <p> The implications extend well beyond meteorology . Agriculture and horticulture , pillars of Kashmir 's economy , are especially vulnerable to seasonal irregularities . Apple orchards depend on sustained winter dormancy , and premature warmth risks triggering early budding . If blossoms emerge too soon , they become susceptible to late frosts . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ undo months of growth , placing families reliant on orchard harvests in economic uncertainty . <p> Rice cultivation faces comparable risks . Paddy irrigation depends largely on predictable snowmelt cycles , and diminished snow reserves heighten fears of water scarcity during peak summer months . At the same time , the steady decline of traditional springs , once dependable water sources in rural communities , is reshaping daily life . Villages that historically relied on perennial nags and chashmas now increasingly depend on tanker supplies , a shift that carries financial strain as well as emotional loss . <p> Tourism , another cornerstone of the regional economy , is equally affected . Kashmir 's winter identity is inseparable from snowfall , whether on Gulmarg 's ski slopes or in the iconic imagery of snow-draped landscapes . Reduced snowfall shortens the winter tourism season , affecting guides , hoteliers , and transport workers . The absence of snow alters not only economic patterns but also the cultural image of Kashmir itself . Beyond immediate economic concerns lies a broader ecological narrative . Himalayan mountain systems are warming at a rate faster @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , snowlines shift upward , and new glacial lakes form , each change quietly reshaping the Valley 's environmental trajectory . The unusually warm February thus represents more than a fleeting anomaly ; it reflects a deeper transformation challenging long-standing assumptions of climatic stability in a landscape once defined by dependable seasonal contrasts . <p> These changes also resonate emotionally . For generations , winter has shaped Kashmir 's collective memory and cultural rhythm . Memories of snowball fights , frozen mornings along Dal Lake , and icicles slowly melting under pale sunlight form part of a shared identity . When February begins to resemble April , it disrupts more than temperature records ; it unsettles memory itself . The fading presence of snow becomes a subtle erosion of nostalgia , gently altering stories passed from one generation to the next . There is also a psychological dimension to shifting seasons . Predictable cycles offer reassurance , suggesting that nature follows a familiar script despite life 's uncertainties . When those cycles blur , that sense of continuity weakens . February 's unexpected warmth introduces a quiet anxiety , an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> The phenomenon underscores the interconnectedness of climate and society . Environmental shifts in Kashmir can not be separated from global warming , pollution , and broader ecological pressures . Local irregularities mirror planetary trends , reminding us that even remote mountain valleys are not insulated from global change . February 's warmth thus stands as both a local experience and a global signal . <p> This growing vulnerability calls for urgent and practical adaptation . Strengthening water management , promoting efficient irrigation , monitoring glacier health , protecting wetlands , and reviving traditional water systems are no longer optional but essential to building resilience against climatic uncertainty . At the same time , sustained research and continuous monitoring of snowpack , precipitation , and hydrological patterns are critical to identifying risks before they escalate . While policy and science form the backbone of this response , real resilience will depend on informed community participation . Kashmir 's long history of enduring floods , droughts , and severe winters offers a foundation of strength , provided awareness translates into timely and collective action . <p> February 's warmth also @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in statistics and distant forecasts . Moments like this render it tangible . When pherans feel excessive in February and snowlines retreat into memory , climate change shifts from a remote concept to an intimate reality . The Valley now finds itself at a fragile crossroads . This February 's warmth could remain an isolated anomaly , a temporary disturbance within an otherwise stable climatic pattern . Alternatively , it may signal the gradual normalization of altered seasons , where winter arrives weakly and spring advances prematurely . The uncertainty itself may be the most unsettling aspect , emphasizing the growing difficulty of predicting the future through the lens of past experience . <p> As February yields to March , hope is tempered with unease . Will snowfall return to restore mountain reserves and steady the rivers , or will lingering warmth continue to blur seasonal boundaries ? When February begins to resemble April , the change moves beyond weather ; it reshapes memory , identity , and the fragile balance between people and nature . Kashmir 's beauty has always drawn strength from its distinct seasons , winter 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and autumn 's gold . As these contrasts fade , the Valley remains breathtaking , yet subtly altered . February 's warmth stands not only as an anomaly , but as a quiet reminder that even the most timeless landscapes are vulnerable to change . <p> For now , February 's sunlit afternoons may appear tranquil , even deceptively pleasant . Yet beneath this warmth unfolds a deeper narrative of ecological imbalance , shifting seasonal rhythms , and the pressing need for collective awareness . Whether this February proves an exception or marks the beginning of a new climatic chapter will depend on forces both local and global . Until clarity emerges , the Valley continues its silent dialogue with mountains , rivers , and skies , waiting for winter 's familiar presence to return . In that waiting coexist hope and apprehension , an acknowledgment that when February feels like April , it is not only the weather that has changed , but the very story of seasons itself . <p> The formal recognition of the Disability Caucus within the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is a decisive step toward inclusive ... <p> According to Professor Kevin Anderson , one of the world 's most respected climate scientists , and based upon a 30-year uninterrupted trendline : " We are headed for 3 ? @@135282523 <h> The Future of Forests <p> Our species ' origin and destiny are entangled with the roots and branches of trees . We evolved in and around trees , and we 've learned to breed and plant them for their fruit , nuts , wood , and blossoms , taking their seeds with us as we migrated -- hence the English walnut , native to Persia , and the Georgia peach , native to China . It 's a relationship that has carried us around the globe , often in boats or carts made from trees . <p> While human communities have benefitted immensely from trees , tree communities ( i.e. , forests ) have n't always fared so well in the bargain . In this article , we 'll trace the ups and downs of this relationship and inquire why it has grown more one-sidedly abusive in recent decades . Unsurprisingly , many recent challenges to the health of forests have emerged because of climate change -- even as forests are proving to be one of the planet 's primary climate-stabilizing systems . <p> Finally , we 'll explore @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the face of global warming and other threats . Along the way , we 'll dip into some of the most intriguing recent scientific findings about trees and forests . <p> The Ghosts of Forests Past <p> During recent millennia , the world 's forests have changed in size , composition , and sometimes location . Consider central Europe : During glacial times , the region was mostly treeless ; but starting about 10,000 years ago , with higher temperatures and melting ice came the flourishing of dense oak , lime , and hazel forests , forming a mosaic pattern across the landscape . During this period , human settlements gradually expanded , adding farms , gardens , and pastures to the mosaic . As centuries passed , and as agriculture and metal smelting proliferated , more trees were cut for wood , for fuel , and to clear land for planting annual crops and for pasturing animals . Forests contracted and sometimes expanded according to human priorities . However , by the 16th century , holznot ( German for " wood shortage " ) had become a persistent problem @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and , later , other fossil fuels . Today the ancient central European forest is nearly gone , and its remnants are under threat . <p> North America saw a similar evolution . In 1800 , the region of what is now the southeastern United States was covered by a vast , 93-million-acre expanse of old-growth longleaf pine stretching from Virginia to Texas . This arboreal ecosystem had been carefully tended for centuries by Native peoples , who used managed burning to create clearings among towering , fire-adapted trees . Early explorers recorded extraordinary plant and animal biodiversity in a dense , mature silvan landscape . But by 1820 the forest was facing rapid clearing for settlement , agriculture , and roads , a process that accelerated greatly with the advent of steam locomotives , which initially burned wood for fuel while also lugging timber to distant cities . <p> Altogether , nearly one-third of the world 's forests have been lost over the last 10,000 years , with forest cover on habitable land shrinking from 57 percent to 38 percent ( forests formerly covered 40 percent of Earth 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ) . The pace of loss accelerated greatly in the last century , with half of all historic deforestation occurring after 1900 . <p> Although global deforestation rates peaked in the 1980s and later slowed , they remain high , especially in tropical regions , due to logging and agriculture . But , in the current century , a new threat is emerging that could result in the loss of over half the area of the world 's remaining forests by 2100 from wildfire , drought , flood , and heat stress . <p> Forests as Climate Victims <p> Recent research suggests that climate change will have a range of impacts on forests , most of them destructive . It 's widely understood that tree species that have adapted to conditions prevalent over the past few thousand years will need to migrate toward the poles to thrive in a warmer world . However , forests are lagging up to 200 years behind the necessary rate of migration , raising the prospect of widespread forest collapse . Further , the composition of most forests is shifting toward faster-growing , less resilient @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are becoming younger and shorter -- largely due to the climate crisis but also to the human introduction of non-native trees -- and this is reducing their overall carbon storage capacity . They 're also becoming simpler , populated by fewer species . Unfortunately , the species that appear to be losing out are ones that grow more slowly and anchor forest ecosystems , supporting diverse webs of life -- especially in the tropics , where biodiversity is highest . <p> When fast-growing trees dominate a forest , storms , drought , and pests can cause more damage . Slower-growing , long-lived trees often have deeper roots , sturdier trunks , and denser wood that help forests resist drought and pests . Further , pollinator insects , birds , and mammals are often adapted to slow-growing trees . <p> Finally , due to climate change and shifts in forest composition , wildfires are getting worse , currently burning more than twice as much tree cover annually as they did 20 years ago . Carbon emissions from forest fires increased by 60 percent globally between 2001 and 2023 , with boreal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Particularly in the tropics , forests are facing tipping points where they may become carbon sources rather than sinks due not just to wildfires but also intensified droughts and reduced soil carbon stability . <p> Forests as Climate Heroes <p> As all this is happening , we are learning more about forests ' role in stabilizing the global climate . Trees provide shade , cool the local environment through transpiration , moderate global water cycles , and remove carbon from the atmosphere . Through these four benefits , forests offer perhaps our best realistic hope for minimizing the climate crisis . <p> You 've surely noticed that it 's cooler to sit under a tree than to stand in blazing sunlight . That 's why cities with more trees enjoy lower surface temperatures in summer months . Forests provide the same service on a vast scale , and as forests are cut , local surface temperatures rise significantly . <p> Forests also cool the land through transpiration . Trees draw water from the soil up to their leaves , where it evaporates . Much of the energy needed to evaporate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that heat energy is transferred to water , the air cools . This is the same mechanism that makes you feel colder when you step out of a pool . <p> A single tree in a tropical forest can cool local land and air equivalent to the work of two household air conditioners , evaporating up to 150 gallons of water per day . Forest canopies cover a large surface area , which can evaporate millions or billions of gallons a day . When forests in tropical regions are cut down , this evaporative cooling stops , and the land surface warms . This is happening with the enormous Amazon rainforest , and the consequences will be global . Borneo is seeing a similar pattern . In 2018 , researchers surveyed people in 477 villages , and found that the villagers clearly understand that deforestation on the island is resulting in hotter temperatures that threaten the health of their families . <p> With all that evaporation going on , you might think forests would have a net drying effect on the surrounding land . But the opposite is true . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cycles to keep soils moist year-round . Meanwhile , tree roots minimize erosion and provide habitat for beneficial soil organisms . Forests reduce weather extremes ( including droughts and floods ) and maintain conditions that benefit not only trees themselves , but the entire web of life in sylvan ecosystems . <p> Trees also remove carbon and store it in their roots , trunks , branches , and leaves . Altogether , the world 's forests store roughly 860 billion tons of carbon in their biomass , deadwood , litter , and soil . As a critical carbon sink , they actively absorb a net 7.6 billion tons of CO2 annually -- about 1.5 times more than the United States emits each year . <p> " The substantial body of research we review reveals that forest , water , and energy interactions provide the foundations for carbon storage , for cooling terrestrial surfaces , and for distributing water resources . Forests and trees must be recognized as prime regulators within the water , energy , and carbon cycles . " <p> The Intelligence and Resilience of Trees <p> As we @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ maintaining stable , habitable environments , we 're also beginning to appreciate trees ' intelligence , sociality , and resilience . Research reveals that trees form complex , interdependent networks that enable them to both cooperate and compete . <p> While some scientists maintain that " intelligence " implies conscious thought in brains -- which plants , of course , do n't have -- Canadian forestry scientist Suzanne Simard argues that the complex , agency-driven behavior of trees constitutes a form of intelligence . Trees express this intelligence through communication , memory , and resource sharing . <p> Trees communicate both below and above the ground . Under the soil surface , they connect their roots via fungi , allowing them to share nutrients . Research suggests this network ( the " Wood Wide Web " ) can , in some cases , transfer nutrients from older " mother trees " to younger seedlings . Trees also send chemical and electrical signals root-to-root , prompting neighbors to prepare for threats like disease or drought . Above ground , trees release volatile organic compounds ( VOCs ) into the air when @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to strengthen their defenses by producing tannic or phenolic compounds . <p> In addition to communicating , trees sense their environments in ways we 're just beginning to understand . Recent studies suggest trees can react to the sound of running water or the vibrations of pollinator wings . Simard and German forester and author Peter Wohllebenposit that trees can learn from past experiences , such as droughts , and make decisions about resource allocation . Dying trees even seem to know the future : before they expire , they warn their offspring to start making new root connections . <p> Much of this recent forest research focuses on the role of large , old trees acting as hubs in arboreal networks , nurturing young trees and maintaining forest stability . Simard contends that mother trees are anchors of forest communities , and are remembered by other trees after they die . <p> What We Can Do for a Forested Future <p> The intelligence of trees creates and maintains resilient arboreal communities . If we humans are to survive , we must similarly build and restore our own resilient communities @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ benefit from them . But for that to happen , humanity must begin treating the forest as more than just a monetarily valuable resource . <p> Given the current accelerating rate of destruction , our top priority must be to defend native forests and the mother trees that anchor them . Globally , the most dedicated forest defenders are Indigenous peoples , who according to some estimates currently protect 80 percent of the world 's biodiversity . In the Brazilian Amazon , Indigenous communities ' efforts to assert collective land rights have reduced deforestation by 66 percent . In Sumatra , Farwiza Farhan ( co-founder of HAkA , an NGO protecting the Leuser Ecosystem ) has confronted illegal palm oil companies to protect old-growth forests . In Zambia , Honorary Forest Officers ( HFO ) protect the Imanda mushitu forest from illegal logging and inspire the next generation of conservationists . In Nigeria , Forest Guards risk their safety to stop poachers and loggers , offering a first line of defense against forest destruction . <p> Beyond forest defense , our next priority must be reforestation . While major global @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Bonn Challenge ( aiming to restore 350 million hectares ) attract significant funding , community-driven efforts in the Amazon , Madagascar , and Indonesia often achieve their goals with lower cost ; such efforts depend on the work of dedicated campaigners like Leah Namugerwa of Uganda , a youth climate activist . <p> However , it 's essential to consider where we should be planting trees in a warming world . This can start with forecasting the likely future climate regime for areas targeted for reforestation efforts and then planting trees that will thrive in that climate ; in effect , helping forests migrate . A 2026 study found that strategic planting with future climate considered , such as in Canada 's boreal forest edge , could significantly boost carbon removal . <p> More thought must also be given to the kinds of trees being planted . Commercially driven reforestation efforts often focus on fast-growing species that yield straight , easily milled timber . However , this results not in a forest ecosystem but in a tree plantation . In recent decades , tree plantations have been growing in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ native forests are far better for climate change remediation and maintenance of biodiversity . We should be planting more slow-growing native trees , in mixed patterns that reproduce healthy , self-sustaining ecosystems -- and that requires creating habitat for animal species that have evolved with native forests . Like all other organisms , trees depend on relationships : with other plant species , and with pollinators and seed spreaders . Holistic reforestation programs in Nevada , Oregon , and Idaho , as well as proponents of " mini-forests , " are taking steps in this direction . <p> In 2023 , about 84 billion dollars were spent globally on reforestation and forest protection . This year , roughly 700 billion dollars are likely to be spent just on AI data centers . Humanity would get by just fine without AI , as we have done for 99.999 percent of our history . But without trees , humans may not persist . <p> The future of forests and that of humanity will be intertwined , like our pasts . The decisive question facing us is : Will it be a balanced @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to failure ? <h> Subscribe to Our Newsletter <p> Richard Heinbergis Senior Fellow of Post Carbon Institute , and is regarded as one of the world 's foremost advocates for a shift away from our current reliance on fossil fuels . @@135282532 <h> Managing Water Differently : Algeria Facing Hydrological Extremes <p> What if , in Algeria , water were no longer seen solely as a scarce resource to exploit or a threat to control , but as an ecological and economic capital to preserve and develop ? <p> Across the country , the same paradox is emerging : prolonged droughts and declining groundwater levels , punctuated by sudden , devastating floods . In a matter of hours , entire neighborhoods in Algiers , Oran , B ? ja ? a , or Skikda can be submerged , while a few weeks later , water restrictions are imposed . This contradiction is not merely a climate problem -- it reveals a deep disruption between Algerian territories and their natural water cycles . <p> Coastal cities : impermeable surfaces and vulnerability <p> Along the coast , where the majority of the population and economic activity is concentrated , rapid urbanization has drastically transformed landscapes . Soils have been sealed with concrete , rivers and streams buried or diverted , and floodplains built over . As a result , rainfall no longer infiltrates , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and causing sudden floods . Each heavy rain is a stark reminder : cities drown when it rains , yet dry out when it does n't . <p> Meanwhile , these cities rely on distant dams , costly transfers , and increasingly energy-intensive desalination . Much of the rainfall , which could be harnessed locally , is lost to the sea . <p> High Plateaus : erosion , runoff , and stressed agriculture <p> Between the Tell Mountains and the Sahara , the High Plateaus are fragile and strategic . Rainfall is irregular but often intense , while degraded soils struggle to retain water . Runoff carries fertile soil away , silts up dams , and limits aquifer recharge . <p> Agriculture consumes most of the available water , often with practices ill-suited to arid conditions . Overpumping further depletes groundwater while productivity remains low . Without major landscape and agricultural transformations , the High Plateaus risk becoming mere runoff corridors from the mountains to the sea . <p> Sahara : fragile oases and illusory abundance <p> Farther south , the Sahara sometimes gives the illusion of abundant water thanks @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ non-renewable at a human timescale , are being extracted faster than they recharge , threatening the sustainability of oases and local ecosystems . <p> Sponge landscapes : a strategy for Algeria <p> To address these imbalances , the concept of a sponge landscape offers a coherent and contextually relevant approach . It envisions the entire territory -- from urban rooftops in Algiers and Oran , to the High Plateaus , to desert oases -- as a living system capable of slowing , storing , infiltrating , and redistributing water . <p> In cities , this means permeable surfaces , infiltration parks , rainwater harvesting , and restoring urban streams . In agricultural and steppe areas , it involves hedges , soil cover , agroforestry , stone bunds , half-moons , and terraces to retain water and regenerate soils . In the Sahara , it entails rehabilitating oases , protecting palm groves , modernizing traditional water systems , and capturing every drop of rainfall . <p> Together , these measures create a " breathing " system capable of reducing floods , limiting erosion , replenishing shallow aquifers , and securing water @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hydrological extremes in Algeria , the question is no longer whether this transition is desirable -- it has become urgent . The challenge is to embed it in public policy : urban planning , agriculture , river management , desertification control , and water governance . In short , designing territories that no longer repel or waste water , but retain it and build the country 's future with it . <h> Subscribe to Our Newsletter <p> El Habib Ben Amara is an architect and urban designer from a tribal ksar ( fortified oasis ) in Algeria . @@135286903 <p> In 2015 , the global community adopted the United Nations Sustainable Development Agenda , outlining 17 Sustainable Development Goals ( SDGs ) to be achieved by 2030 . These goals represent humanity 's collective commitment to end poverty , protect the planet , and ensure prosperity for future generations . While many sectors contribute to these goals , forests occupy a uniquely central position . They sustain water systems , regulate climate , support biodiversity , and provide livelihoods to millions . <p> India , with nearly 24.62 per cent of its geographical area under forest and tree cover according to the Forest Survey of India , stands at a critical juncture . The nation 's forests support the livelihoods of over 275 million forest-dependent people , many of whom live in remote and economically vulnerable regions . From the perspective of a forest administrator working closely with field realities , it is clear that forest departments are not merely custodians of trees ; they are institutions that connect environmental stewardship with human welfare . Achieving the SDGs in India will require the integration of scientific forest management with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and Ecosystem Protection <p> At the heart of forestry lies the mission of conserving life on land , directly aligned with SDG 15 : Life on Land . India is among the world 's 17 megadiverse countries , hosting nearly 8 per cent of the world 's recorded biodiversity . Forest departments safeguard this wealth through protected areas such as national parks , wildlife sanctuaries , conservation reserves , and community reserves . <p> The role of the forest department is therefore evolving from enforcement to partnership . Community-based protection committees , local monitoring groups , and participatory forest management have demonstrated success in reducing illegal logging , forest fires , and wildlife poaching . When communities recognise that a thriving forest secures water , soil fertility , and cultural identity , conservation becomes a shared responsibility . <p> Climate Change Mitigation <p> Climate change is one of the greatest challenges of the 21st century . Forests act as natural climate regulators by absorbing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and storing it as biomass , directly contributing to SDG 13 : Climate Action . India 's forests currently store an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has committed under the Paris Agreement to create an additional carbon sink of 2.5 -- 3 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent through forest and tree cover by 2030 . <p> Forest-fringe communities are often the first to observe changes in rainfall patterns , rising temperatures , and declining water sources . When they participate in afforestation programs , protect plantations , and prevent forest fires , they become frontline actors in climate action . Forest departments can strengthen these efforts by integrating local participation in afforestation drives , climate-resilient species selection , and landscape restoration initiatives . <p> Water Security <p> Forests function as natural water towers . They capture rainfall , recharge groundwater , regulate stream flows , and prevent soil erosion . In a country where water scarcity is becoming a critical challenge , these ecological services are invaluable . <p> This directly supports SDG 6 : Clean Water and Sanitation . Studies indicate that over 70 per cent of India 's major rivers originate in forested watersheds . The health of rivers such as the Ganga , Brahmaputra , Godavari , and Cauvery is closely linked to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Villagers living near forests play a crucial role in maintaining these watersheds . Preventing forest fires , avoiding overgrazing , and protecting vegetation along stream banks can significantly improve water availability . Awareness programs conducted by forest departments help communities understand the connection between forests and drinking water security . <p> Poverty Reduction and Rural Livelihoods <p> For millions of rural families , forests represent more than ecological assets ; they are a source of daily survival . Collection of fuelwood , fodder , honey , medicinal plants , and other non-timber forest products forms a significant part of the rural economy . Sustainable forest management therefore contributes directly to SDG 1 : No Poverty and SDG 2 : Zero Hunger . <p> In many tribal and forest-fringe regions , income from forest products supplements agricultural earnings , particularly during lean seasons . Forest departments can strengthen this relationship by promoting value addition , training communities in sustainable harvesting techniques , and facilitating market access . When villagers see forests as a sustainable source of livelihood , conservation becomes economically meaningful . <p> Green Economy and Employment <p> The concept @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ strategies . Forests offer opportunities for sustainable growth through eco-tourism , bamboo-based industries , herbal medicine production , and nature-based enterprises . <p> These activities contribute to SDG 8 : Decent Work and Economic Growth . Across India , eco-tourism initiatives managed jointly by forest departments and local communities have generated employment while promoting environmental awareness . Young people from forest-fringe villages are increasingly finding employment as nature guides , wildlife trackers , eco-tourism operators , and conservation volunteers , creating a generation that views forests as assets to be protected . <p> Gender Inclusion and Community Participation <p> Women have traditionally been at the forefront of forest resource management in rural India . @@135303654 <p> India 's children are facing a new health reality with frequent illnesses linked to climate change . What used to be a predictable calendar of seasonal sniffles has evolved into a year-round cycle of fever , fatigue , and respiratory distress . Parents are increasingly finding that the old rules of recovery no longer apply , with children falling ill more frequently and taking longer to bounce back . While it is easy to attribute this to a general lack of immunity , experts suggest that the root cause is much broader . The rapidly shifting climate is rewriting the rules of public health , and children are standing on the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , ranging from searing heatwaves to sudden , intense downpours and persistent winter smog , are becoming frequent disruptors of daily life . For a child whose immune system is still in the crucial stages of development , these environmental shocks create a constant state of physiological stress . This connection between climate volatility and paediatric health was a central theme in a recent initiative by the Savlon Swasth India Mission , which included expert insights shared on The Doc 's Pod , hosted by journalist Faye D'Souza . <p> As Dr. Bhaskar Shenoy , Consultant Pediatrician at Manipal Hospital , Bengaluru , points out , a child 's immune system functions optimally in stable conditions . The current reality of sudden weather transitions and pollution spikes forces their developing bodies to work overtime , often leaving them vulnerable to infections . <p> The rising cost of environmental stressThe impact of climate change on health is tangible and varied across seasons . In recent years , large swathes of north and northwest India have grappled with temperatures soaring past 45 -- 50 ? C. This extreme heat has led to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ school-going children . Furthermore , the heat alters behaviour ; families retreat indoors to escape the sun , often into poorly ventilated spaces where viral infections can circulate more easily . Paediatric centres in cities such as Bengaluru and Pune have noted a correlation between prolonged heat spells and persistent respiratory issues . <h> Live Events <p> The risks shift but do not diminish with the arrival of the rains . In states such as Assam , Bihar , and Himachal Pradesh , monsoon waterlogging inevitably compromises water sources , leading to spikes in diarrhoeal diseases . Winter brings a different threat in the form of smog , where particulate matter inflames young airways , triggering asthma flare-ups and throat infections . Meals rich in seasonal vegetables , whole grains , and proteins provide the essential vitamins , such as iron and zinc , that immune cells require to function . Minimising ultra-processed snacks helps reduce systemic inflammation , while ensuring access to boiled or filtered water during the monsoon is critical to preventing gut infections that can weaken immunity long-term . <p> ET Spotlight <p> The hygiene shield : Hygiene is the most effective tool for breaking the chain of transmission . Dr. Shenoy emphasises that hands remain the primary vehicle for germs , regardless of the season . Establishing a non-negotiable routine of handwashing before meals , after play , and upon returning from school can drastically reduce the incidence of both respiratory and gastrointestinal infections . <p> However , the modern environment demands that hygiene extends beyond just hands . <p> Surface hygiene : Regularly using a surface disinfectant on high-touch areas ensures that germs do not linger in the home . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ harbour bacteria , especially after active play or gym sessions .
