@@135390796 <h> Climate resilience : Why the lived experiences of people should guide policy responses to heat waves <p> Heat is not only a physical phenomenon , but is experienced through how people interpret risk in their daily lives . <p> Summary <p> How people actually experience rising heat should shape the policies meant to protect them . This way , policy efforts can move beyond reacting to temperature spikes and start responding to the real adversities of health , income constraints and energy insufficiency that households face . <p> As the India Meteorological Department warns of above- normal temperatures across much of India in the coming weeks , the country is once again preparing for a hotter summer . But for many Indians , rising heat is more than a seasonal forecast ; it shapes everyday life . <p> Climate change is no longer an abstract environmental challenge . It is experienced through heat stress , illness , income loss and rising energy costs . In cities such as Delhi , rising temperatures are already reshaping daily routines , from when people work and travel to how households cope inside @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ between climate ambition and ground outcomes . This gap widens when policies and programmes are not designed around how people actually experience heat in their everyday lives , masking the uneven , neighbourhood-level realities of heat risk and vulnerability . <p> Delhi 's Heat Action Plans , like many across India , are still primarily guided by ambient temperature data and emergency response mechanisms . This makes a strong case for placing citizen-centred evidence at the heart of effective and equitable climate action . <p> A report by Artha Global , Mapping Heat Inequality across Neighbourhoods in Delhi , showcased that even when reported temperatures are uniform across a city , climate risk is experienced very differently across households ; exposure is shaped by micro-climate conditions and urban form ( density , building materials , tree cover and access to open spaces ) , while coping capacity and outcomes are determined by socioeconomic characteristics and access to adaptation measures such as cooling appliances and technologies . <p> Neighbourhood-level patterns show how urban design shapes everyday heat exposure . Areas where built-up land rises from around 25% to 55% can experience @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , raising tree cover from just 3% to 11% can lower temperatures by nearly 1 ? Celsius , suggesting that even relatively small gains in urban greenery can significantly cool local environments . <p> But heat , as we know , is not only a physical phenomenon -- it is experienced through how people interpret risk in their daily lives . Existing datasets can map exposure , but they can not explain how households cope , adapt or make trade-offs . <p> Insights from other behavioural research show that climate impacts are weighed against income , mobility , safety and social obligations ; and when heat is understood as a threat to earnings rather than only to health , responses shift dramatically . <p> This helps explain why many adaptation efforts struggle to take root . The barrier is rarely lack of awareness ; it is the pull of everyday habits , financial constraints and slow institutional response . Citizen-centred surveys are , therefore , essential to capture not only where heat is experienced , but how people actually respond to it . <p> Artha Global 's study conducted primary @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and the coping strategies people adopt . Its findings show that extreme heat acts as a structural stressor : a 3 ? Celsius rise in experienced temperature ( from 42 ? to 45 ? Celsius ) corresponds with a 15% increase in the number of respondents reporting instances of illness lasting over five days . Additionally , the temperature increase also corresponded to a 10% jump in households missing work ( from 18% to 28% ) . <p> Coping capacity , however , is deeply unequal . The study demonstrated that households with air-conditioners reported significantly lower work loss than those without . Wealthier householders already ran air-conditioners for around 12-14 hours a day ( during the peak summer months ) , while lower asset households lacked both -- access to cooling and the financial ability to increase electricity use . <p> This inequality is reflected in energy spending : wealthier households spend nearly twice as much on electricity , not only because they can own more appliances , but because they can afford to use it more intensively to protect themselves from heat . <p> These findings lead to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ lived realities and not just temperature data . Institutionalizing citizen experience means creating routine systems to collect and use neighbourhood-level data on health effects and coping alongside technical climate metrics . <p> This evidence can guide heat action plans ( HAPs ) , shape early warning thresholds and direct investments in cooling , green cover and energy support to the communities that need them the most . <p> Agencies such as the National Disaster Management Authority ( NDMA ) , National Research Development Corporation ( NRDC ) and BSES Yamuna Power ( as well as other power distribution companies ) have an opportunity to operationalize this shift by embedding citizen data into disaster preparedness , adaptation programmes and grid planning . <p> Making lived experience a part of official climate evidence shifts policy from reacting to heat to responding to how people actually live with it . 
@@135390851 <p> A vendor sells cold drinks on a hot summer day at a market in Karachi in May . AFP <p> When the daytime air feels like an oven and night brings no relief , people in Karachi , Pakistan , say the heat " goes straight to the head " . They mean more than dizziness or sweat . <p> It 's the creeping panic of a body that can not cool down : restless nights , frayed tempers , a household on edge . Here , a heatwave is not simply a matter of high temperatures . It 's a public health emergency that seeps into every corner of life : physical health , sleep , mood and the invisible care work that keeps families and neighbours alive . <p> For families living on informal and unstable incomes and in fragile housing , such heat is not just uncomfortable ; it can be deadly . <p> Heatwaves occur when temperatures push daily highs past 40 degrees celsius inland and above 35 degrees celsius on the coast . In 2015 , a single heatwave killed more than 1,200 people @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the quieter psychological toll which is rarely counted in official statistics builds with every wave of extreme heat . <p> In our research , residents describe lying awake in stagnant air , waking drenched in sweat and starting the next day already exhausted . Sleeplessness makes emotions harder to manage , fuelling conflict in homes stretched thin . Many , especially women , speak of a sense of suffocation and dread ; fearing their bodies wo n't cope or that a loved one will collapse . For people with asthma or anxiety the symptoms are magnified , and mothers often feel an acute worry for children and elderly relatives . <p> Play <p> This mental strain is no overreaction , it reflects harsh realities . Outdoor workers lose wages when extreme heat makes it unsafe to stay on the job . At the same time , food and water prices climb as supply chains falter and demand spikes , just as family incomes shrink . Hospitals and clinics can be difficult to reach because high temperatures often lead to power cuts , overloaded transport systems and an increase in heat-related @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Women often shoulder the heaviest burden because in many households , especially in low- and middle-income countries , domestic and caregiving duties still fall largely to them . Social norms often expect women , not men , to stay home with children , care for older relatives and organise water or food supplies . When a heatwave strikes , those tasks become more physically demanding and more time-consuming : fanning overheated children through sleepless nights , checking constantly on elderly neighbours , and answering calls for help . <p> In low- and middle-income countries , women also face disproportionate health risks from climate change , particularly during extreme heat , precisely because these gendered roles and socio-cultural expectations expose them to greater stress . The unpaid labour that holds households together -- caring , fetching water , preparing food -- is carried mainly by women . As one Karachi resident explained , on the hottest days she and her neighbours watch over pregnant women : " Women here may be poor , but they support each other , sharing water , looking after each other 's children and cooking for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " <p> Such neighbourly care surfaces again and again . Families pool money to buy safe drinking water when supplies run short . In some informal settlements , one of the most immediate ways people cope with rising heat is by increasing their reliance on water , often through hand pumps that serve as vital lifelines during prolonged heatwaves . Neighbours check on older people during power cuts . Women take turns cooking when kitchens become unbearable for elderly or pregnant relatives . These are not feel-good tales of " bouncing back , " but acts of collective survival : immediate , exhausting and often invisible . They reveal how vulnerability is shaped by poor housing , patchy healthcare and weak governance -- factors that leave people exposed when crises strike . <p> Extreme heat also compounds heat related health risks and financial costs . In crowded settlements and displacement camps , food spoils quickly , appetites wane and clean water becomes harder to find and more expensive to acquire . Pregnant and breastfeeding women struggle to maintain nutrition . International research shows that heat stress can deplete micronutrients , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ premature childbirths . When these pressures collide with poverty and displacement , the dangers of malnutrition and long-term harm can only grow . <p> Residents ' requests are strikingly simple . They want electricity that stays on through the night , clean water that they can afford and clinics that remain open when symptoms worsen . These are not luxuries . They are the difference between anxiety and peace of mind , between starting the day rested or already exhausted . <p> Even small interventions help : a working fan , a shaded community space , advice on hydration and sleep . Women-led groups already organise water-sharing , neighbour check-ins and shaded play areas . Strengthening these networks , and centring polices on women 's health could save lives and protect mental health during future heatwaves . <p> Counting only hospital admissions or heat-stroke cases misses what people say matters most : a child kept hydrated , a safe place to sleep , the absence of panic on the hottest days and nights of the year . These everyday markers of dignity and survival are where real adaptation begins . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ stop the sun . But we can stop each other from being alone in the heat . " <p> Gulnaz Anjum is Assistant Professor of Climate Psychology , Centre for Social Issues Research , Department of Psychology , University of Limerick .

@@135392194 <p> India 's new Solid Waste Management Rules , notified in January 2026 , aim to replace the decade-old 2016 framework from April . <p> The rules introduce a centralised digital portal for registration , reporting and tracking waste flows across the country . <p> They also strengthen environmental standards , auditing systems and polluter-pays mechanisms . <p> However , questions remain over institutional capacity , data reliability and the ability of local bodies to implement the new framework . <p> This is the first of a two-part series . <p> The Union Ministry of Environment , Forest and Climate Change notified a new set of Solid Waste Management ( SWM ) Rules in January 2026 . Set to replace the decade-old 2016 framework on April 1 , 2026 , these regulations introduce a sharper focus on digital traceability , standardised reporting and rigorous auditing . <p> While the environmental intent is clear , the transition from fragmented local reporting to a centralised national architecture raises a critical question : Can a standardised digital portal effectively manage the layered , informal and varied realities of India 's waste ecosystem ? @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ new Rules transition from fragmented , non-standardised reporting to a mandated , standardised compliance architecture . At the core of this transition stands a centralised digital portal . The Rules require mandatory registration of all obligated entities -- bulk waste generators ; urban and rural local bodies ; sorting and processing facilities ; waste-to-energy and furnace-based industries ; and every landfill site . Engagement with unregistered entities is explicitly prohibited . <p> All registered facilities must submit periodic reports , while the portal functions as a single national point for tracing waste flows . Aggregated data will be publicly available through dashboards , signalling an intention to make compliance transparent and traceable , even if the full spectrum of operational data may not be accessible to the public . <p> While operational guidelines from the Central Pollution Control Board ( CPCB ) are still awaited , the ambition of the Rules and the portal raises several practical concerns . The Rules state that entities may register through local bodies , assuming a uniform administrative capacity that rarely exists . Recent years of digital monitoring through the Swachhatam Portal -- a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Bharat Mission activities -- have demonstrated the variability in administrative capacity even among India 's urban local bodies . <p> Beyond questions of integration and capacity lies a deeper concern about the quality and credibility of the data that will populate the portal , highlighting the importance of standards and a robust audit system . <h> Standards and audit system <p> The 2026 Rules maintain strict environmental standards for water and air quality at landfills , compost quality and incineration emissions . Notably , they introduce a graded classification system for refuse-derived fuel . All processing entities are legally bound to comply with these standards , along with any technical protocols issued by the relevant authorities . <p> However , the central question remains : how will these standards be enforced , and how will the authenticity of self-reported data be verified ? <p> The Rules assign both responsibilities to the State Pollution Control Boards ( SPCB ) . The earlier Rules had similar mandates , but with limited success . To bridge the historical capacity gap within SPCBs , the new Rules rely on a recently introduced institutional mechanism @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ notified on August 29 , 2025 , the ministry introduced authorised Environment Auditors as a supplementary compliance mechanism , describing it as a step towards trust-based governance . These auditors are expected to conduct facility audits to ensure compliance with prescribed standards and verify the reports submitted by local bodies and private operators . However , the operational framework for authorising and registering these auditors is still awaited through further guidelines . <h> Polluter Pays Principle <p> The Rules reaffirm the polluter-pays principle as the financial backbone of the compliance framework . Local bodies are reminded of their responsibility to levy and collect user fees sufficient to cover operational expenditure and to periodically report these expenditures . <p> The introduction of the Extended Bulk Waste Generator Responsibility ( EBWGR ) certificate is a significant addition . By requiring bulk generators to trade certificates or directly fund waste processing , the EBWGR mechanism aims to offset the financial burden currently borne by municipal budgets . <p> For non-bulk waste generators , the responsibility for fee collection remains with local bodies . Policy discussions have repeatedly suggested linking user fees with other @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> The Rules also introduce an Environmental Compensation ( EC ) mechanism for entities operating without registration , submitting false information , or manipulating compliance reports . SPCBs are authorised to collect EC following CPCB guidelines , while local bodies may levy compensation on bulk waste generators and continue to impose spot fines and penalties on other waste generators . <p> However , questions remain regarding how these funds will ultimately be utilised . Experience with existing environmental compensation mechanisms under other waste rules suggests that utilisation rates remain low in many states . Without clear mechanisms to transfer and reinvest these funds into strengthening waste management systems , the corrective intent of environmental compensation may remain limited . <p> Ultimately , the effectiveness of polluter-pays mechanisms will depend on whether financial responsibility translates into meaningful fiscal support for institutions . <h> Defined timeline <p> Defined timelines were among the most consequential features of the Solid Waste Management Rules , 2016 . They required local bodies to create infrastructure , prepare strategies and develop waste management plans within stipulated periods . <p> The 2026 Rules retain the importance of timelines @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ compliance windows of 18 , 24 and 36 months depending on population size , with larger cities expected to comply first . State governments are required to prepare state-level strategies within one year , while all local bodies must frame or update their byelaws by March 2027 . <p> What is noticeably absent are the explicit infrastructure deadlines that characterised the earlier Rules . The 2016 framework required the establishment of waste processing facilities within two years , sanitary landfills within three years and remediation of dumpsites within five years . While many of these targets were not fully achieved , they provided clear benchmarks for infrastructural progress . <p> The new Rules shift the focus towards periodic reporting and monitoring cycles , with quarterly disclosures and annual reports becoming central to compliance . While this shift may strengthen oversight and transparency , it also raises questions about the capacity of local institutions to meet these reporting requirements .

@@135405745 <p> In every corner of modern life , from skyscrapers to sneakers , waste is a silent by-product of design decisions . In a world generating over 2.24 billion tonnes of municipal solid waste1 annually , with nearly one-third inadequately managed , design is no longer just about aesthetics or function ; it is about responsibility . <p> As climate change accelerates and natural resources grow increasingly scarce , engineers and designers are being confronted with a more urgent question : how to create without destroying . The answer is emerging through zero-waste design , an approach that challenges conventional production models and places sustainability at the very heart of innovation . <p> Yet the question arises : what if the very way things are designed eliminates waste before it is ever created ? That is the promise of zero-waste design , a fast-emerging discipline at the intersection of engineering , creativity , and sustainability . What was once considered an idealistic concept is now a practical , measurable strategy with real environmental and economic impact . And as this approach continues to gain momentum , it is redefining how @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ More than Just a BuzzwordTraditionally , the world followed a ' linear ' economy : take raw materials , make products , use and throw them away . Today , with climate change and resource shortages pressing urgently on societies everywhere , designers and engineers are shifting towards a ' circular ' economy . Here , materials stay in use longer , products are made with end-of-life recycling in mind , and waste is reduced at every stage of the lifecycle . <p> At its core , zero-waste design is more than recycling ; it represents a reimagining of how products , systems , and spaces are conceived so that nothing ends up in landfill . It involves selecting materials that can be reused or safely returned to nature , designing products that can be easily repaired , disassembled , or upgraded rather than discarded , and optimising manufacturing processes so that offcuts and by-products are minimised or repurposed . <p> In many cases , it improves efficiency and reduces long-term costs by lowering material consumption and disposal fees . Companies adopting these principles often discover that sustainability drives innovation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ utilitarian garments across many cultures were created through zero waste practices . Examples include the Japanese kimono and the Indian saree . Even in ancient Greece and Rome , clothing was typically made from loosely draped rectangles or other simple shapes that did not waste much , if any , fabric . <p> Key techniques and some of the examples are as follows : <p> Zero-Waste Pattern Making : Designers create pattern layouts that fit together like a jigsaw puzzle across the fabric width , ensuring near-100 per cent material usage . Instead of trimming excess fabric , the garment 's design adapts to the cloth , turning efficiency into a creative constraint . <p> Subtraction Cutting : Developed by Julian Roberts , this experimental technique focuses on the negative space ( the holes cut into fabric ) rather than traditional pattern pieces . The result is bold , sculptural silhouettes created from continuous fabric with minimal waste . <p> 3D Knitting / Whole-Garment Technology : Garments are knitted directly into their final shape in a single seamless piece . This eliminates panel cutting , offcuts , and assembly waste @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Zero-Waste Draping : Fabric is draped directly on a mannequin in ways that preserve the entire textile piece . This intuitive approach encourages fluid forms and ensures that no material is discarded during construction . <p> Upcycling and Patchwork : Leftover scraps and deadstock fabrics are transformed into new garments or accessories . For example , UK-based Palava uses production leftovers creatively , proving that waste materials can become valuable design elements . <p> Historical Techniques : Many traditional garments were inherently zero-waste long before modern sustainability movements . The kimono and saree , for example , are constructed from uncut or minimally cut fabric , demonstrating that resource-efficient design has deep cultural roots . <p> These techniques show how zero-waste fashion blends innovation , craftsmanship , and tradition to dramatically reduce textile waste without compromising creativity or style . <p> Engineering Principles Behind Zero WasteZero-waste design in engineering means integrating sustainability into the DNA of a product or structure , from material selection to eventual reuse or recycling . <p> Key principles include : <p> Design for Material Efficiency : Engineers carefully analyse how materials are cut , shaped @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Advanced Computer-Aided Design ( CAD ) and simulation tools help optimise layouts and structures so that materials are used precisely where they are needed ; and nowhere else . <p> Closed-loop Systems : Zero-waste engineering prioritises closed-loop systems , where materials remain in circulation instead of being discarded . Products are designed so their components can be easily disassembled , repaired , reused , or recycled at the end of their life . This approach not only conserves raw materials but also reduces the environmental cost of extraction and processing . <p> Technology-assisted Optimisation : Digital technology plays a crucial role in making zero-waste goals achievable at scale . Engineers use digital modelling , artificial intelligence , and real-time data to predict waste before it occurs and adjust processes accordingly . Sensors embedded in production lines can track material usage , energy consumption , and by-products , allowing teams to intervene instantly when inefficiencies appear . <p> In manufacturing , for example , companies use IoT ( Internet of Things ) sensors and analytics to monitor waste streams in real time , allowing precise interventions that cut waste and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ precision , supported by smart technology , can transform sustainability from an abstract ideal into a measurable , achievable outcome . <p> Fashion and Zero WasteZero-waste design is reshaping fashion beyond buildings and products . Traditionally , garment manufacturing generates enormous amounts of textile waste . Often , between 15 per cent and 30 per cent of fabric2 is discarded during the cutting process alone . Globally , this adds up to millions of tonnes of waste each year , much of which ends up in landfills or is incinerated . <p> Zero-waste fashion challenges this model at the design stage . Instead of cutting patterns that leave behind scraps , designers use advanced cutting techniques and digital pattern optimisation to ensure that every centimetre of fabric is accounted for . Some zero-waste garments are designed like puzzles , where pattern pieces interlock perfectly on the fabric surface , leaving no leftovers . In many cases , these methods can reduce fabric waste by up to 90 per cent compared to conventional production . <p> Technology plays a critical role in this transformation . Digital design software allows designers to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ single piece of fabric is cut . This not only minimises waste but also reduces the need for physical samples , saving time , energy , and materials . Increasingly , artificial intelligence tools are being used to optimise layouts automatically , balancing aesthetics , fit , and efficiency . <p> Importantly , zero-waste fashion proves that sustainability does not require sacrificing creativity or style . On the contrary , many designers view the constraints of zero-waste principles as a catalyst for innovation , leading to distinctive aesthetics and thoughtful craftsmanship . As consumers become more aware of fashion 's environmental impact , zero-waste design is emerging not just as a responsible alternative , but as a defining feature of the industry 's future . <p> By making sustainability a design criterion , engineers and creatives can pioneer solutions that are not only efficient , but also responsible and future-ready . It also encourages businesses to rethink supply chains , production methods , and product lifecycles in ways that conserve resources and reduce costs over time . As consumers become more environmentally conscious , companies adopting zero-waste practices are also @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Ultimately , zero-waste design is not just an environmental strategy ; it is a forward-looking approach that aligns innovation , economic resilience , and planetary well-being . <h> Conclusion <p> Zero-waste principles are not just for big corporations or architectural firms . From choosing products with recycling programmes to supporting companies that embed circular economy thinking into their design processes , every choice matters . Small shifts in consumer behaviour -- such as repairing items instead of replacing them , opting for durable products , or supporting sustainable brands -- can collectively drive significant change . <p> When individuals , designers , and industries work towards the same goal , the impact multiplies across supply chains and communities . Ultimately , embracing zero-waste thinking is about recognising that thoughtful design and responsible consumption together can shape a more sustainable future . <h> FAQs <p> Zero-waste design is an approach that eliminates waste at the design stage by ensuring materials are fully utilised , reused , or returned safely to nature . @@135424935 <h> When Earth became a snowball : The incredible story of survival and life 's comeback <p> Imagine a time when the blue planet looked nothing like it does today . This is not science fiction , but a real time in Earth 's past , a time referred to as the " Snowball Earth " period . Scientists believe that between 700 and 600 million years ago , Earth underwent a time of extreme glaciation . New research is helping us understand how Earth survived these extreme times and how it may have contributed to the emergence of complex life . <h> Snowball Earth explained : When the planet froze over <p> The ' Snowball Earth ' hypothesis , as proposed by Caltech geologist Joe Kirschvink , indicates that there were global glaciations during the Cryogenian period , approximately 700 to 600 million years ago , such that ice sheets reached as far as the equator . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the presence of glacial deposits in areas that are currently considered to be tropical , which should not occur under normal climatic conditions.From geological studies , it has been indicated that once ice sheets expanded to a certain point , a strong feedback cycle took hold . This is due to ice having a reflective quality , so as more of the planet became frozen , more solar energy was deflected , resulting in a further drop in temperature . <p> This ice-albedo effect likely triggered a runaway glaciation that resulted in a planetary icebox , according to researchers at Utah State University.This led to a frozen world with glaciers covering the continents and the potential for an ice-wrapped ocean . <h> What caused Snowball Earth ? However , some models suggest parts of the ocean may have remained unfrozen , then there would have been climate activity.This led to the debate about the fully frozen Snowball Earth , as opposed to the partially thawed Slushball Earth . <h> Life during a frozen Earth : Survival against the odds <p> A global ice age of this scale prompts the following query : How did life manage @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ under ice cover or in deep ocean environments due to life 's adaptation to such extreme environments . For instance , nutrients resulting from glacial erosion might have fueled a growth spurt in marine life , which could have led to more complex life forms . <h> How did Earth escape the deep freeze <p> One of the greatest mysteries about Snowball Earth is how the planet eventually warmed up . @@135425704 <p> Grasslands around the world are quietly changing under pressure from overgrazing , cropland expansion , climate change and biological invasions . In India 's Thar Desert , these pressures are reshaping which species survive and how they share space . <p> A new ecological study finds that two invasive forces , fast-spreading mesquite trees and free-ranging dogs linked to human settlements , are changing how native mesocarnivores ( medium-sized carnivores ) move , hunt and coexist in this landscape . <p> " Wildlife communities of the Thar Desert remain relatively understudied even as the landscape undergoes rapid ecological change , " says Chetan Misher , a wildlife ecologist at the Wildlife Conservation Trust and the study 's corresponding author . <p> " Mesquite has become the dominant woody plant , altering habitat structure , while free-ranging dogs function as apex or dominant predators in many areas . Together , these invasives are reshaping native communities through habitat modification , changes in predation , competition and interference , with cascading effects across the ecosystem , " <h> Changing landscape <p> The Thar spans about 446,000 square kilometres across western India @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ parts of western Rajasthan and the Kachchh region of Gujarat . <p> To capture ecological variation across this landscape , researchers focused on two contrasting sites for the study : the mesquite-dominated Banni grasslands of Gujarat and the more fragmented , agriculture-influenced grasslands around Bikaner in Rajasthan . <p> Both regions support similar wildlife , including desert and jungle cats , desert and Indian foxes , golden jackals , along with a wider range of desert-adapted small mammals , birds and reptiles . The researchers conducted field surveys using motion-triggered infrared camera traps to record wildlife presence and activity . <p> The study also used high-resolution satellite imagery to map land cover , including open vegetation , invasive woodland , agriculture , water bodies and built-up areas . These habitat layers were linked to each camera location across multiple spatial scales . Using occupancy modelling , the study estimated where carnivores were likely to occur while accounting for missed detections and environmental influences . The study also use temporal activity analysis to examine when species were active and how much their daily routines overlapped . <h> Winners and losers in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ foxes avoided areas used by desert foxes or dogs . But they were often found where golden jackals were present , in contrast to a study from Maharashtra where Indian foxes avoid jackals . <p> Jungle cats also frequently appeared alongside jackals . Desert foxes and dogs were recorded more often in Bikaner , whereas jackals and jungle cats were more common in mesquite-dominated Banni . Indian foxes were not detected in Bikaner , while desert cat detections were similar in both regions . <p> Desert foxes strongly preferred open native vegetation and avoided mesquite woodland and farmland . They were also frequently found close to human settlements , likely because villages in Bikaner lie near the remaining grassland patches they depend on . <p> Golden jackals , as habitat generalists that can thrive in diverse environmental conditions , used a wide range of environments and persisted even where the mesquite expanded . Indian foxes , the smallest canid in the study , avoided desert foxes and dogs and disappeared from Bikaner altogether , suggesting possible competitive exclusion where predator and dog pressures are high . @@135426440 <h> Global Recycling Day 2026 : History , Significance , and Theme <h> Share : <p> X <p> Global Recycling Day , observed every year on March 18 , was established by the Global Recycling Foundation in 2018 . The day was created to highlight the crucial role recycling plays in preserving the planet 's natural resources and securing a sustainable future . Over time , it has gained international recognition , encouraging governments , industries , and individuals to adopt responsible waste management practices . <p> The history of recycling itself dates back centuries , when communities reused materials out of necessity . However , modern recycling became more structured during the 20th century with the rise of environmental awareness . Events like the Earth Day 1970 helped bring global attention to pollution and waste , eventually leading to organized recycling systems . <p> The significance of Global Recycling Day lies in its message that waste is not just garbage -- it is a valuable resource . Recycling helps reduce landfill waste , conserve energy , and minimize pollution . For example , recycling paper saves trees , while @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ plays a key role in combating climate change by lowering greenhouse gas emissions . <p> Each year , the day is guided by themes that emphasize innovation , action , and awareness . A common focus is recognizing recyclables as the " Seventh Resource , " alongside water , air , oil , natural gas , coal , and minerals . This concept encourages people to view everyday waste -- like plastic bottles , paper , and metal -- as materials that can be reused rather than discarded .

@@135427039 <p> The Western Indian Ocean and Eastern Central Atlantic are experiencing the fastest rise . <p> For over three decades , satellites orbiting Earth have measured the height of the ocean surface with remarkable precision . These measurements are crucial because changes in ocean height are one of the clearest indicators of how our planet is responding to climate change . Rising ocean surfaces signal warming temperatures , melting ice and shifting ocean currents . <p> These all directly affect coastal communities through flooding , erosion and habitat loss . Even a small rise in the baseline sea level means that normal tidal cycles and storm surges reach further inland . This can turn high tides into damaging flood events . <p> Many people assume ocean levels are uniform , like water sitting flat in a bathtub . In reality , the ocean surface is surprisingly uneven . Winds push water in certain directions . Ocean currents redistribute heat . Temperature differences cause water to expand or contract . Even variations in Earth 's gravity field create bumps and dips in the sea surface . @@135427481 <h> Lost in Ice : The long journey of MATS 1107 <p> 18-Mar-2026 <p> <p> Mangsatabam Dinachandra MeeteiIn the remote mountains of Alaska , glaciers move slowly but steadily , carrying with them the silent records of the past . Beneath one such glacier lay the remains of a tragic air crash that occurred more than seven decades ago . The story of Douglas C-124 Globe-master II flight MATS 1107 is not only a tale of aviation disaster but also a reminder of how nature can hide history for generations.A Routine FlightOn November 22 , 1952 , the large military transport aircraft departed from McChord Air Force Base near Seattle . Its destination was Elmendorf Air Force Base near Anchorage , Alaska . On board were 52 passengers and crew members . Some were traveling to new postings in Alaska , while others were preparing for deployments related to the Korean War.At 7.53 p.m. , the crew made their final radio contact using the call sign MATS 1107 . At that moment , nothing seemed un- usual . But the harsh weather of Alaska soon began to alter the course @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the aircraft away from its intended route . As the plane drifted north , it lost contact with important radio navigation signals that would normally help guide the crew back on track.Flying through darkness and poor visibility , the aircraft unknowingly approached the steep slopes of Mount Gannett , a towering 9,629-foot peak in Alaska 's rugged Chugach Mountains.At around 8.15 pm , the plane crashed into the mountainside at high speed , just about 50 miles from its destination . The impact was devastating . The massive aircraft , weighing about 175,000 pounds , likely broke apart almost instantly.The crash triggered an avalanche that swept fragments of the plane nearly 1,000 feet down the steep slope . The wreckage was scattered across the upper reaches of Colony Glacier.The Wreckage DisappearsA search plane spotted the wreckage several days later . However , severe storms soon covered the crash site with fresh snow . Rescue operations became impossible , and the search was eventually called off.Over time , thick layers of snow continued to fall over the site . In the years that followed , as much as 300 feet of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ compressed into solid ice , trapping the remains of the aircraft deep within the glacier.A Glacier in MotionGlaciers are not still masses of ice . They move slowly downhill under their own weight . As Colony Glacier flowed toward lower ground , it carried the hidden wreckage along with it . Each year the ice moved several hundred feet , silently transporting pieces of the aircraft through the frozen valley.Decades passed , and the crash faded from public memory . Yet beneath the glacier , the remains of the aircraft continued their slow journey.Through the Ice FallSometime during the 1980s , the buried wreckage likely passed through the Colony Ice Fall , one of the most turbulent sections of the glacier . Here the ice plunges nearly 3,000 feet down a steep slope and breaks into enormous blocks.These blocks , sometimes as large as apartment buildings , collide and crack as the glacier moves . In this violent environment , pieces of the aircraft would have been crushed , scattered , and mixed with the shifting ice.For the families of those on board , the glacier had become a vast @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to lower and warmer elevations , the surface ice began to melt each summer . The glacier gradually lost several feet of thickness every year.This melting slowly brought the deeply buried wreckage closer to the surface . After many decades , fragments of the lost aircraft began to reappear from the ice.A Story That May Still DisappearToday , Colony Glacier continues to slide toward a large lake at its base . If the glacier carries debris from the crash into the lake , some remains may sink to the bottom and be lost forever.At the same time , scientists warn that glaciers around the world are melting faster due to climate change . While melting ice may reveal hidden traces of the past , it may also erase them before they can be properly recovered.Memory Preserved in IceThe story of MATS 1107 shows how powerful natural forces can preserve history in unexpected ways . For more than seventy years , the glacier slowly carried the wreckage down the mountain , protecting its secrets beneath layers of ice.Although the passengers and crew never reached their destination , their story continues to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ waiting to be remembered .

@@135439227 <h> A Statement of Concern -- Part 5 : Keep the Climate , Change the Economy <p> To tackle climate change , the global outlook must change from " Gain maximisation for a few " to " Risk minimisation for all . " Capitalism will not do this as it supports profit maximisation for the fat cats . A sustainable society has to be equitable as well , and sustainability has to be global . Eco-anarchism ( a mix of eco-socialism and anarchism ) is the alternative that can make society sustainable and equitable , and one that has transparent , democratic grassroots governance . The transition to eco-anarchism will be very bumpy and uneven in time and space , the roadmap for which is still hazy . Unlike past thinking , a sustainable and equitable society can be ushered in by a rainbow coalition of working people -- wage labour , farmers , indigenous people , women , youth , gig workers , etc . <p> Global outlook change required <p> Capitalism failed to tackle climate change as it followed the line " Keep the economy , let the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cats to continue making profits . Had it realised that the climate is more important than the economy , it would have followed a diametrically opposite line , i.e. , " Keep the climate , change the economy . " But that would have meant forsaking profits , for which global outlooks need to change from " Gain maximisation for a few " to " Risk minimisation for all species . " <p> A sustainable society has to perforce be equitable also . If surplus ( profits , capital ) is usurped by a small elite , the rest will also aspire to emulate the elite , and the never-ending vicious cycle continues . Sustainability , therefore , has to be universal . A sustainable society in one village or one nation will find it difficult to survive . Capitalism is threatened by a sustainable nation , as the growth of its profits will be curtailed . Sustainability has to be a global project . <p> What kind of society can deliver equity and sustainability ? Hunting-gathering societies were , to a large extent , equitable and sustainable . Since @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ equitable and sustainable . The Soviet Union and China , and other " socialist " countries , aspired to be equitable , but they did not aspire to be sustainable . Cuba was forced to make some moves to become a sustainable society in the last decade of the 20th Century due to the collapse of the Soviet Union and the loss of their cheap fossil fuel source . <p> Eco-socialism , which holds sustainability and equity to be equally important , and elements of anarchism that argue for self-governing small communities and a minimalist state , show promise in becoming societies that are sustainable and equitable . A combination of eco-socialism and anarchism may be termed eco-anarchism . In addition to ushering in equity , sustainability and community governance with a minimalist state , eco-anarchism has the potential to eliminate growth generated by capitalism and anthropocentrism . However , such a society is yet to take birth , so we do not know how it will function in practice . <p> Eco-anarchism requires four fundamental requisites : <p> Reducing global energy consumption <p> Moving into a global energy and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 2050 and relying on solar , biomass , other renewable and animate energy <p> Shifting from non-renewable materials to renewable biotic resources <p> The transition from capitalism to eco-anarchism will be extremely uneven in time and space . Unless there is a civilizational collapse , social change will not happen at the same time or even in the same way all over the world . Capitalism is likely to react forcefully , and even violently , to change , as happened in the aftermath of the Russian Revolution . @@135441808 <p> Rising global temperatures due to climate change could push millions of people into physical inactivity by 2050 , potentially leading to hundreds of thousands of premature deaths and billions of dollars in lost productivity , according to a modelling study published in The Lancet Global Health . <p> As the planet warms , increasing heat is expected to limit people 's ability to remain physically active . Physical inactivity is already a major global health concern , with nearly one in three adults failing to meet the World Health Organization ( WHO ) guidelines for weekly exercise . <p> The study analysed data from 156 countries between 2000 and 2022 to project how rising temperatures may influence physical activity levels through 2050 . <p> Findings suggest that for every additional month with an average temperature above 27.8 ? C , physical inactivity could increase by 1.5 percentage points globally and 1.85 percentage points in low- and middle-income countries , while showing no significant impact in high-income nations . <p> This rise in inactivity is projected to result in an estimated 470,000 to 700,000 additional premature deaths annually , along @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> The impact is expected to be most severe in already hot regions , including Central America , the Caribbean , Eastern Sub-Saharan Africa , and Equatorial Southeast Asia , where inactivity levels could rise by more than 4 percentage points for each additional month of extreme heat . <p> However , researchers caution that these findings are based on modelling and self-reported physical activity data , and only account for temperature changes . As such , there remains uncertainty about the precise real-world effects . <p> The authors stress the need for urgent action to mitigate the health impacts of rising temperatures . <p> Recommended measures include designing cooler , climate-resilient cities , improving access to affordable air-conditioned spaces for exercise , and providing clear public guidance on staying safe during extreme heat . @@135460141 <h> The geography of business presence is being transformed by the reality of climate stress <p> Corporate property is especially exposed to climate change-related risks because it is designed to last . <p> Summary <p> Business site decisions are fast becoming climate bets , with the long-term value of corporate property at stake . As heat , floods and infrastructure stress intensify , location choices are driven by the environmental risks that real estate valuations increasingly face . <p> India 's corporate skyline has expanded rapidly over the past three decades . Tech campuses in Bengaluru and Hyderabad , logistics parks along the Delhi-Mumbai industrial corridor and multiple warehouse clusters on city outskirts reflect a country building the infrastructure of a modern economy . Yet , much of this expansion has been planned around connectivity , labour access and land prices . Climate risk has rarely figured in the blueprint . <p> The 2015 Chennai floods offered a stark illustration , causing industrial property losses estimated at around ? 14,600 crore , according to a report on building climate resilience for Indian industry . Events like these are not isolated @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ embedded in the built-up environment . <p> Corporate property is especially exposed because it is designed to last . Office parks , warehouses and campuses are typically built with a life-span of 30-50 years . Once a facility is constructed in a vulnerable location , the investment is effectively locked in . Flood-prone land , rising temperatures or fragile infrastructure can gradually erode the reliability of assets that companies depend on for operations . <p> Extreme heat has emerged as one of the most pervasive pressures in recent times . India 's cities can be as much as 6 ? Celsius warmer than surrounding rural areas because of the urban heat island effect , as research by World Resources Institute shows . <p> For large corporate campuses and data-heavy office buildings , this translates directly into higher electricity consumption for cooling . Power systems designed for milder conditions can come under severe strain during prolonged heatwaves . <p> Logistical infrastructure faces a different kind of exposure . Warehouses and distribution hubs are often located on the edges of cities where land is cheaper and access to highways is easier . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Heavy rainfall can overwhelm drainage systems , cut road access and damage inventory . As supply chains become more time-sensitive , even short disruptions can ripple through corporate operations . <p> Risks extend beyond physical damage . Climate stress increasingly affects the economics of property assets . Cooling costs rise as temperatures climb . Insurance premiums may increase in areas with repeated disasters . Worker productivity falls when heat becomes extreme . The Institute of Risk Management estimates that heat-related productivity losses already cost India tens of billions of dollars annually and could threaten several percentage points of GDP by the end of this decade . <p> Investors are beginning to treat these pressures as financial variables rather than environmental concerns . Property portfolios are increasingly assessed for exposure to physical climate hazards such as floods and heatwaves , according to the OECD , a club of rich nations . For companies with large real estate footprints , resilience may soon matter as much as location . <p> That shift is beginning to influence how corporate infrastructure is planned . One response is better information . Companies are starting to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , avoiding sites prone to floods or extreme heat exposure . The practice is already visible in sectors such as data centres , where developers increasingly factor climate risks into site decisions . <p> Building design is also evolving . India 's policy framework for construction emphasizes structures that can withstand rising temperatures and other climate stresses . Architects are turning to techniques that reduce heat absorption and cooling demand , including reflective materials , improved ventilation and building orientation that minimizes solar exposure . Flood-prone sites are increasingly incorporating raised foundations and improved drainage . <p> Green infrastructure is another emerging tool . Expanding tree cover and permeable landscapes can lower local temperatures and absorb excess rainwater during storms , urban adaptation research supported by the International Finance Corporation shows . Corporate campuses that integrate parks , shaded walkways and natural water retention areas not only improve work conditions for staff but also reduce flood risk . <p> Even logistics infrastructure is beginning to adapt . Developers are building warehouses that meet green certification standards , which often include better insulation , water management systems and more efficient energy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ quadruple by the end of the 2020s as institutional investors push for more resilient assets , according to JLL , a property consultancy . <p> India 's corporate real estate boom is far from over . New industrial corridors , tech clusters and logistic networks will continue to reshape its landscape . However , the next generation of corporate infrastructure will be judged not only by how efficiently it supports growth , but by how well it withstands the pressures of a changing climate . <p> Companies that treat resilience as a design principle rather than an afterthought may find that their safest assets are also the most valuable . In the coming years , corporate India 's geographical map may be shaped as much by climate science as by economics . <p> The author is an independent expert based in New Delhi , Kolkata and Odisha . @@135462237 <h> Bhumi Suposhan : Enriching Soil <p> Soil is the most important and indispensible living natural resource . No form of life is possible without this resource . As a living resource , it is one of the most bio-diverse habitats on Earth hosting more than 50% of the planet 's species . A single teaspoon of healthy soil can contain between 10,000 and 50,000 different species of micro-organisims . A single gram of soil can contain billions of bacterial cells and miles of fungal hyphae . It is estimated that only 1% of soil microorganism have been identified or successfully culture in laboratory settings . Soil micro- organisms can break down certain contaminants . Soil is not a dead thing as perceived by most of us . Infact it is a living entity constituting a critical component of the natural system and is an important contributor to the human wealth through its contribution to food , water and energy security and as a mitigator to biodiversity loss and climate change . Soil is the foundation of every terrestrial food chain on Earth . As soil is the ultimate natural @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ survive without it . Healthy soil is thus a sine qua non , it is an essential condition and absolutely necessary for everything to exist and that exists on this planet . Unfortunately the crude and unscientific farming of last so many decades with indiscriminate use of synthetic fertilizers and plant protection chemicals have left the soil unhealthy , thirsty and in a poor state of affairs . The soil has lost its fertility , vigour and microbial diversity . The climate change and various anthropogenic activities have also degraded our soil , put excessive pressure on our water resources . Various issues the soils face include : <p> Soil Erosion : The floods , cutting of trees and faulty agronomic practices leads to soil erosion thereby depriving the land of its topmost fertile soil . Soil erosion refers to removal of the top layer of soil by various means which include both anthropogenic as well as natural events . The natural agents responsible for soil erosion include wind , water and waves . Among these agents , water is considered as the main cause of soil erosion . Soil @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ nutrients content decline as they are washed away by erosion , underground water level also gets reduced , vegetation and habitat loss , frequent occurrence of drought and floods and many other adverse effects . <p> Soil Salinization : Another issue is the Soil Salinization . Soil salinization is a major process of land degradation that decreases soil fertility and is a significant component of desertification processes in the world 's dry land . The accumulation of soluble salts in soil occurs when evaporation exceeds precipitation and salts are not leached but remain in the upper soil layers in low-lying areas . It is estimated that by 2050 , around 50% of the soil will be affected due to salinity without any fruitful mitigation techniques to overcome the situation . Besides reducing net cultivable area , soil salinization hits hard the productivity and quality of agricultural produce , quality of water , the choice of cultivable crops , the biodiversity and ultimately the livelihood security of the people . Arid and semi-arid regions , where evaporation rates are high and fresh waters are scanty to flush out the excess salts @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Water logging : Similarly water logging occurs when there is no proper drainage system in the fields . They become waterlogged and this result in the saturation of crops wherein the normal circulation of air is not possible and the amount of oxygen in the soil declines . <p> Shifting/Jhum cultivation : Shifting cultivation is a type of cultivation practiced mainly in North-Eastern states of India is actually a type of slash and burn method of cultivation wherein the forest land is cleared for cultivation of crops . This causes deforestation , environmental pollution , loss of habitat for wild animals etc . The burning of forest also results in soil erosion and gradual degradation of soil . <p> Besides faulty agricultural practices like excessive tillage , monocropping , indiscriminate use of chemicals also adversely affect the soil health . The microbial count as well as diversity has been drastically reduced . The collapse of soil microbial diversity leads to degradation of conventional agro-ecosystems . In the country , nearly 147 million ha of land is subjected to soil degradation including 94 million ha from water erosion , 23 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , 9 million ha from wind erosion and 7 million ha from a combination of factors due to different forces . The Government of India has also fixed a target of restoring 26 million ha of degraded lands , including salt-affected soils , by the year 2030 to ensure food security for the people . Estimates suggest that every year nearly 10% additional area is getting salinized and by 2050 , around 50% of the arable land would be salt-affected . Situation is alarming and we have to act urgently to ensure that things do not go to a point of no return . Estimates suggest that to feed the burgeoning population , the country would require about 311 million tons of food grains ( cereals and pulses ) by 2030 and this requirement would further increase to 350 million tons by 2050 when India 's population would be around 1.8 billion . Restoring and maintaining soil health is thus very important . As food security is a major concern , any lapse on our part can have catastrophic consequences . @@135473827 <p> Geopolitics in capitalism is greatly shaped by energy and raw material availability , technology , production systems , finance and markets . Of these factors , energy plays a central role . Power in 2025 flows through pipelines , transmission lines , shipping lanes , semiconductor cleanrooms , digital networks , and financial institutions . The states that command these systems will control the immediate future . <p> The rivalry between the United States and China is fundamentally about control of technology , production systems and markets . Russia 's war in Ukraine reveals how energy markets are weaponised . The Middle East demonstrates the enduring centrality of oil even in an energy transition . <p> Capitalism has failed to solve the problems of inequality and sustainability . Fossil fuels and 80 critical non-renewables will be exhausted before 2100 . None of the renewable energy sources can completely replace fossil fuels . The energy transition from fossil fuels to renewables has been sluggish . Global warming is out of control and threatens to overwhelm society before this century end . <p> Many civilisations in the past have collapsed due to energy collapses . Capitalism today faces the same prospect , and this collapse will be global . The only solution is for the world to power down and agree on an equitable regime for the use of energy and other raw materials . <p> ENERGY PRIMER <p> Primacy of Energy <p> Energy is the mover and shaker of all processes in the universe . Without the play of energy , the universe will be in a dead state , and all processes , abiotic and biotic , will come to a dead halt . Natural history is the study of how energy flows shaped the evolution of the universe . <p> All life forms require energy for their survival . Species other than humans take only as much energy as they require for their survival and reproduction , the latter requiring only a small fraction of the total energy used by the species . <p> Humans have the ability to understand how energy has shaped nature ( science ) . Humans used energy to extract raw materials and fashion them into goods and services ( technology ) . No other species on earth can do this . Over time , scientific and technological knowledge grew . In the last three centuries , growth was exponential , as was the harvest of energy and raw materials to produce goods and services . <p> Social history is the description of how human society has changed over time in its working and structure , consequent to the use of an increasing amount of energy and raw materials to make and consume artefacts and services , thereby altering the environment . <p> EROEI <p> All land and water produce energy as photosynthesis occurs amidst them . Some lands and water bodies are better endowed geologically and climatically to produce energy , e.g. , fertile valleys and estuaries in tropical countries , and consequently have greater biodiversity , support higher human populations , and have older civilisations . <p> Energy from photosynthesis is in the form of food and fuel , and material in the form of fibre and wood . Other large available energy sources are : animate ( animal and human ) , fossil fuels , wind , solar , geothermal , wave and tide , gravitational , and nuclear energy . Harvesting energy from any energy source , including solar energy , requires an energy input . For example , for obtaining fossil fuels , energy is required for prospecting , extracting , transporting , and sometimes refining them . Harvesting food crops using solar energy requires preparing a field and inputting other necessities . <p> The ratio of the energy obtained from an energy source to the energy invested to obtain it is known as the EROEI ( Energy Return on Energy Invested ) . The higher the EROEI of an energy source , the lower the energy cost per unit of energy , and the greater the ease and preference of obtaining it . Energy from fossil fuels has a higher EROEI than biofuels and is therefore preferred to the latter . <p> EROEI of an energy source can increase with technology upgrades . For example , farm technology improvements in the early and middle ages increased the EROEI of food crops . However , the EROEI of an energy source may drop if it becomes harder to obtain . The EROEI of coal was as high as 80 in the early 20th Century but dropped to 20-30 in the 21st Century as it became harder to get to coal seams . <p> Surplus Energy -- Generation , Acquisition , Accumulation <p> If 1 Joule ( J ) of energy is spent to produce oil ( EROEI = 20 ) , the investor of that energy obtains oil containing 20 J , 19 of which is surplus energy . The generation of surplus energy occurs because the harvested energy contains considerably more energy than the energy invested to obtain it . <p> Social development is possible only if there is surplus energy . Surplus energy is one of the material bases for the economic categories of surplus value , profit and capital . No other species on earth can create surplus energy . <p> By virtue of having invested 1 J , the investor acquires the entire harvested energy , i.e. , 20 J. S/he then claims ownership of all the energy s/he has acquired , including the surplus energy of 19 J. <p> Out of the 20 J , if s/he now invests 2 J to produce more oil , s/he will get 40 J worth of oil through the same technology , i.e. of identical EROEI , of which 38 J is surplus energy . The investor now accumulates surplus energy that can be converted into capital or wealth . <p> The process is similar to investments of monetary capital in the production process that leads to the generation of profit in monetary form . This process can go on ad infinitum under the capitalist production system . Here , this surplus energy obtained in the sphere of production can be exchanged in the market to be converted into monetary form , or capital stock or wealth . The UN System of Environmental Economic Accounting recognises this and treats energy ( and other natural resources ) at par with physical capital . <p> Embodied Energy <p> The energy required to produce a product or service in the entire supply chain is known as its embodied energy . In this way , the ' value ' of a good or service is proportional to its embodied energy . For example , a car is more expensive than a cycle because a cycle requires more raw materials and energy . Embodied energy that has the potential to help generate more embodied energy ( means of production ) is one of the material bases for the generation of surplus energy , as the energy invested to harvest an energy source includes embodied energy in the form of machinery , etc. ( means of production ) . In the above example , 1 J includes the flow of energy , such as electricity , the energy to produce the coal that produced the electricity and so on , besides the depreciation in the ' value ' of the machine that was used in the process of producing 20 J of oil . <p> Acquiring and Accumulating Surplus through Conquest and Colonialism <p> Since ancient times , the conquest and colonising of alien lands was a way to seize raw materials and surplus energy in the form of crops and capture embodied energy in the form of wealth and artefacts , and subjugate humans from the conquered territory to create additional food crops and artefacts for further and subsequent appropriations . <p> In 1532 , Spanish marauder Pizarro captured the Inca emperor , Atahuallpa , by defeating his 80,000-strong army with just 168 horse-mounted Spaniard soldiers with cannons , muskets , steel spears and swords , and wearing chainmail armour . Superior knowledge of metallurgy and horses gave the Spaniards an advantage &amp; to extract the largest ransom ever . <p> In the 200 years between the mid-18th and 20th centuries , vast areas of Asia , America and Africa , having about a third of the world 's population was colonised by European powers . The colonial powers usurped a massive amount of surplus generated in these continents . <p> Vasco de Gama landed in Calicut in 1498 . China , India and the Arabs had ships that were as good as or better than European ships . European ships had a stern post rudder that gave them maneuverability , a mix of different types of sails on their three masts that gave them greater speed , and strongly built hulls that made them capable of withstanding more punishment . In sea battles , soon after the Europeans landed in India , they were able to outmaneuver Indian ships and outgun them , as the Indians had not yet mastered the use of ship-mounted cannons despite possessing them . The Europeans soon extracted tribute from the Indians and the Arabs for using the sea lanes . <p> In the last 3 centuries , colonial powers -- British , Dutch , and French were able to extract huge energy surpluses in the form of raw materials , and by producing goods in offshore factories that had low costs . The British Empire thrived because it was able to harvest energy resources from its vast colonies in both the old and the new worlds . <p> Acquiring and Accumulating Surplus through Unequal Exchange <p> The sunlight energy that contributes to photosynthesis in crops is not valued , whereas energy inputs , e.g. , fossil fuels and electricity that contribute to the production of agro inputs , e.g. , farm machinery , agrochemicals , are priced and their price contributes to the cost of farm machinery . However , in energy equations of farm produce , energy in sunlight is considered as an input energy , which then contributes to the energy content of the farm produce . <p> This results in an anomaly between the economic equation and the energy equation for farm produce . In the economic equation , the sun 's contribution is not considered , as it is costless , while in the energy equation , it is captured . This allows the industry sector to do an unequal exchange of energy with the agricultural sector , hence monetarily benefiting . The harvesting of any energy source has an energy cost . In the case of fossil fuels , the cost of fossil fuels is the price paid for prospecting , extracting , transporting and refining them . In the case of sunlight that goes into crops , energy is expended to prepare land for the crops , etc , which is not counted . <p> The agriculture sector is at a permanent disadvantage vis- ? -vis the industrial sector , as there is unequal exchange of energy between these sectors . In short , among the various ' value additions ' taking place in the agricultural sector , only those that are attributed to labour and machinery are counted for in the economic equation . Likewise , the Global South that exchanges crops for industrial products from the Global North is in an unequal exchange of energy with the latter . Hence , continuous to remain backward in comparison to the Global North . <p> Bourgeoises Economics Encourages Unsustainability and Inequality <p> By not costing sunlight , which is a sustainable source of energy and costing fossil fuels and nuclear energy , economics encourages unsustainability . Fossil fuels and nuclear energy are unsustainable , as fossil fuels will be exhausted in about 100 years , and uranium ore in about 150 years . However , since fossil fuels and nuclear energy are costed , these forms of energy are preferred to solar energy as they will add value and fetch the products and services using them a higher price than if solar energy is used , hence will be preferred over solar energy . <p> Energy and Carbon Inequality <p> Private ownership of surplus energy and embodied energy in the means of production , conquest of territories , colonialism and unequal exchange because sunlight is not costed , whereas other energy sources are costed , has led to a significant gap in the per capita energy consumption between and within capitalist countries . This reflects in the gap between income and wealth between the rich and the poor -- nations and people . The per capita energy consumption in various countries and regions is given in the table below . <p> Carbon inequality reflects the same pattern as energy inequality . The rich emit significantly more per capita CO2 than the poor , and are therefore responsible for global warming . <p> Who Owns Surplus and Embodied Energy ? <p> Surplus energy and embodied energy may be owned privately , jointly , collectively , by the state or a legal person such as a corporation or an association . In hunting-gathering societies , the small amount of surplus and embodied energy was held collectively . In a class society , slavery , feudalism , capitalism , surplus , and embodied energy are largely privately owned . In socialism , they are socially owned , but held largely by the state . In communism , it is envisaged that they will be held socially . <p> The question to ask is how much energy was expended to make oil that yields 1 J of energy , and who expended the invested energy . The answer is nature . Nature baked dead biota at high temperatures in its crust for 300 million years to make fossil fuels . <p> The energy that nature used to make fossil fuels is many orders of magnitude more than the 1 J invested to acquire ( prospect , extract , transport , and refine ) fossil fuels from nature . The embodied energy is fossil fuels is ancient sunlight . So , who should fossil fuels belong to -- nature or the humans who acquired them ? <p> Human Labour is an Energy Conversion Process <p> Human labour is an energy conversion process similar to a heat engine , like a prime mover . Likewise , the economy is also a heat engine . Energy is therefore a more basic category than labour , and more useful to understand the exploitation of nature by humans and that of the working class by the bourgeoisie . <p> The economy also does energy conversion and therefore should be treated as a heat engine to understand its working . <p> Mode of Production <p> The manner in which surplus energy is generated , acquired and accumulated is the same in all modes of class societies -- slavery , feudalism and capitalism . The form in which surplus is generated , acquired and accumulated varies in each mode . The mode of production debate that occurred a few decades back looked only at the form and not at the process of surplus generation , acquisition and accumulation . <p> ENERGY IN HISTORY <p> Energy , not money , ideas or institutions , is the fundamental driver of social change . Across millennia , the scale , density , and efficiency of energy capture have shaped population size , economic output , political organisation , and technological complexity . Without changes in energy regimes , major civilizational shifts would have been impossible . Human progress is best understood as a succession of energy transitions . <p> Hunting-Gathering Societies <p> In hunter-gatherer societies , the energy used was limited to human power and biomass , i.e. , wood . The daily energy budget of individuals depended on food gathering and hunting , constraining population densities to very low levels . Because energy flows were small and diffuse , social organisation remained relatively egalitarian and mobile . Such societies were efficient within their ecological niches but incapable of supporting large cities , standing armies , or complex states . For example , Palaeolithic communities relied entirely on muscle power for hunting large animals and on wood fires for cooking -- an energy regime that limited surplus production and thus restricted social stratification . <p> Agricultural Societies <p> The transition from hunting-gathering to agriculture that occurred about 10,000 years ago was marked by a profound increase in usable energy . By domesticating plants and animals , humans began appropriating a far larger share of photosynthetic output . Fields of wheat or rice concentrated solar energy into storable grain , while domesticated cattle and horses multiplied human mechanical power . This shift dramatically raised human population densities and enabled permanent settlements . Early agrarian civilisations in Mesopotamia , China and India are examples of how irrigation and animal traction expanded energy capture beyond what human muscles alone could achieve . <p> Animal power in particular represented a decisive amplification of work capacity . A single ox could deliver several times the sustained power of a human labourer , making large-scale plough agriculture feasible . In medieval Europe , the heavy plough and horse collar improved energy efficiency in farming , allowing cultivation of heavier soils and boosting yields . Though biomass -- wood for heating , charcoal for metallurgy -- remained central to human existence , agricultural societies commanded layered energy flows : human , animal , and plant-based . These surpluses supported cities , specialised crafts , bureaucracies , and imperial states . <p> Agrarian civilisations were ultimately constrained by the limits of photosynthesis . Land area capped energy availability ; deforestation and soil depletion often followed demographic growth . Pre-industrial societies repeatedly approached ecological ceilings . For example , late imperial China and early modern Europe faced wood shortages and pressure on arable land . Economic expansion without new energy sources led to stagnation . And many early civilisations collapsed , and not just stagnated , due to their inability to locate new energy sources , or ways to improve the EROI for the existing sources . <p> Industrial Societies <p> In the transition to industrial society , coal was the first transformative fossil fuel . During the 18th and 19th-centuries , coal replaced wood as the primary source of heat and power in Britain first and subsequently in Europe and later in the rest of the world . The steam engine converted coal 's chemical energy into mechanical motion , liberating industry from reliance on animate , biomass , wind , and water energies . Fossil fuels offered energy densities far beyond traditional biomass , enabling sustained and high economic growth . <p> One example of this transformation is the replacement of charcoal with coke in iron smelting . This innovation dramatically increased steel production , supporting railways , ships , and urban infrastructure . Another is the expansion of rail transport , which multiplied the speed and scale of trade by harnessing coal-fired locomotives . These developments were not merely technological ; they reshaped social organisation , urbanisation patterns , and global trade networks . <p> Oil and natural gas further intensified the fossil-fuel era in the 20th Century . Oil 's high energy density and portability made it ideal for internal combustion engines , revolutionising transportation and warfare . Natural gas improved heating efficiency and became a key feedstock for fertiliser production , boosting agricultural yields through synthetic nitrogen . Modern civilisation -- from skyscrapers to global aviation -- rests fundamentally on fossil energy flows . <p> Energy availability determines the scale of economies , the complexity of institutions , and the capacity for technological innovation . From the muscle-powered bands of hunter-gatherers to fossil-fuelled industrial societies , each leap in energy capture has enabled new forms of social organisation . Without energy transitions , there would have been no agricultural revolutions , no industrialisation , and no modern world . <p> NATION-STATES ' RIGHTS TO DRAW ENERGY FROM THEIR TERRITORY <p> Geopolitics is the interaction between nation-states to assert and defend their rights over territories , or to capture or colonise other states or territories . It is , therefore , important to understand the meaning of a state and a nation , the difference between the two and how they became a hyphenated phrase . Nation-states today jockey for power and influence by cooperating with friendly nation-states and conflicting with others that are deemed unfriendly . This is the essence of geopolitics , and the acquisition and control of energy is at the centre of it . <p> Borders <p> Human-drawn borders , i.e. , other than ecological , geological and climatic ones , demarcate a territory or a space for an individual , a village , a collective , an organisation , a state , or a union of countries . Within this territory , the above entities may acquire the right to harvest , use , and extract raw materials such as energy , water , and other renewable and non-renewable materials . The entity may claim ownership over the territory or may lease it . Entities may defend their rights over the territory either by law or otherwise . <p> States <p> Modern society is built upon the idea of the nation-state , a political form that emerged unevenly across regions but eventually became universal in the 20th Century .
