States existed in early and medieval times in the form of empires based on imperial law ( Roman ) , dynastic monarchies ( Mauryan , Tang , Sahelian ) , religious-imperial ( Aztec , Inca ) , or city-states ( Hellenic ) . <p> After the 1648 " Peace of Westphalia " treaties were signed in Munster and Osnabr ? ck in Germany , the sovereign state was defined as : having political authority over a geographic area with defined territorial borders , being formally equal in diplomacy to other sovereign states , having the right to no interference in its internal affairs by other states , having the right to negotiate treaties directly with other sovereign states . The treaties ended two major wars in Europe , diminished the authority of the Roman Catholic Church over European kingdoms , and brought order to kingdoms that were a jumble of multi-ethnic territories without clear national borders . <p> The 1993 Montevideo Convention on the Rights and Duties of States extends the definition of a sovereign state as having a geographically defined territory with a permanent population with an effective government capable of exercising authority over its territory and entering into relationships with other states independently . <p> The state is a political and legal organisation that exercises authority over a defined territory and population . A state typically possesses institutions such as a government , legal system , military , and administrative bureaucracy . <p> Nations <p> A nation is different from a state . It refers to a community of people who perceive themselves as sharing a common identity based on language , culture , history , territory , or collective memory . A nation is primarily a cultural and psychological community , not necessarily a political one . A nation can exist without political sovereignty , as seen historically in groups like the Kurds spread across several Middle Eastern states , or indigenous populations in various countries . <p> In the 19th Century , nationalism spread across the world , becoming a powerful force in movements for political unification , independence , and self-determination . <p> Nation-State <p> The relationship between nation and state gave rise to the concept of the nation-state , where the boundaries of the political state roughly coincide with the boundaries of a nation . Ideally , a nation-state exists when a culturally unified people govern themselves within a sovereign territory . In practice , however , few states perfectly match this ideal . Many states contain multiple national or ethnic groups , while some nations remain divided across several states . <p> The merging of the nation ( a cultural community ) and the state ( a political entity with sovereignty over a territory ) was historically a gradual process that unfolded between the 17th and 20th centuries in an uneven way across the world . Several major developments -- political , economic , and cultural -- brought the two together to form the modern nation-state . <p> Before the modern era , most states were dynastic empires or kingdoms , where loyalty was to a ruler rather than to the people of the state . The turning point came during the French Revolution with the emergence of the idea that political authority belongs to the people , and not to monarchs , and the concept of the nation was linked to political sovereignty , i.e. , the state . <p> During the 19th Century , governments increasingly undertook nation-building projects to create a unified national identity within their territories , involving standardising national languages , expanding mass schooling and literacy , promoting national histories , myths , and symbols , and creating national armies and bureaucracies . Through these institutions , states actively constructed national identity . <p> Nationalist movements also worked in the opposite direction : instead of states creating nations , nations sought states . In the 19th Century , nationalist movements unified fragmented territories that shared linguistic or cultural identities . For example , nationalist movements led to the unification of Italy in 1861 and Germany in 1871 . <p> In the 19th Century , the merging of nation and state became a global principle through anti-colonial movements . Colonised populations adopted the idea of national self-determination to demand independence from imperial rule . After World War II , dozens of new states emerged , and the nation-state became the dominant model of political organisation worldwide . <p> The alignment between a nation and a state is rarely complete . Many states contain multiple ethnic or linguistic groups , while some nations remain divided across several states . In the 21st Century , as nationalism resurges and global power balances political shifts , the idea of the nation-state continues to shape geopolitics , war , and competition over resources , markets , and identity . <p> The contemporary system of sovereign states is formally organised through institutions such as the United Nations , which enshrines legal equality between states and non-interference in the internal matters of a state . But beneath this legal architecture lies a more turbulent reality . States pursue raw material harvesting , particularly of energy and water , and holding of artefacts ( embodied energy ) from within and outside their territory , and also protect these endeavours with political influence and military security ( both of which require energy expenditure ) . In such a system , nationalism becomes both glue and fuel ; it binds populations together internally while sharpening distinctions externally . <p> Roots of Modern Nationalism <p> As empires fragmented and colonialism disintegrated in the 19th and 20th centuries , the territorial state became a worldwide model , and nationalism became a mobilising force against imperialism . In Asia , Africa , and Latin America , anti-colonial movements adopted the language of national self-determination . By the mid-20th Century , the nation-state had become the universal political unit . <p> In many regions , the state preceded the nation . Colonial borders in Africa and the Middle East enclosed diverse linguistic and ethnic communities within artificial frontiers . After independence , governments undertook nation-building through education , official languages , military service , political and military domination of minority populations in a state by majority populations , and shared historical narratives . Where these efforts succeeded , the nation-state stabilised . Where they faltered , internal divisions persisted . Today 's conflicts often reflect unresolved tensions between imposed territorial boundaries and evolving identities . <p> The Logic of the Nation-State in Capitalism <p> Despite globalisation , digital interconnection , and the growth of international institutions , the nation-state remains the primary actor in world politics . Its legitimacy rests on a collective identity that defines insiders and outsiders . Its security depends on territorial integrity . Its prosperity depends on access to finance , markets and technology , and resource control . <p> Nationalism 's resurgence is not an aberration but a structural feature of a system built on sovereign units . In times of uncertainty -- economic volatility , demographic change , technological disruption -- national identity offers stability and political clarity . Yet the same force can polarise societies and harden interstate rivalries . <p> The nation-state system has brought a measure of order through recognised borders and legal equality , but it has also institutionalised rivalry . As power diffuses and global challenges intensify , the interplay between sovereignty and interdependence will determine whether the 21st Century is defined more by global cooperation or conflict . <p> GEOPOLITICS <p> Under capitalism , geopolitics is about control over natural resources , renewable and non-renewable , e.g. , water , energy , rare earths , etc , and markets . Religious and ethnic differences also play a role , but that is a subject that will not be discussed in this paper . <p> Control of Natural Resources <p> Control over natural resources has long shaped international disputes and conflicts . Water is a critical resource . River basins that cross national borders are potential flashpoints . Dams and upstream diversions can alter downstream livelihoods , transforming hydrological disputes into diplomatic crises . As climate change intensifies droughts and variability , water governance will become more politically charged . <p> In the 21st Century , competition increasingly focuses on critical minerals necessary for digital technologies and renewable energy systems . Lithium , cobalt , nickel , and rare earths are essential for batteries , electric vehicles , and advanced electronics . Control over these supply chains enhances economic and strategic resilience . While outright wars over such minerals have not occurred yet , states have used trade restrictions , investment controls , and diplomatic pressure to secure access to critical minerals . <p> Markets and Economic Access <p> Access to markets is a motive for expansion and conflict . Colonial empires sought not only territory but also captive markets for manufactured goods . Industrial competition in the late 19th and early 20th centuries heightened rivalry among European powers and contributed to the conditions that culminated in global war . <p> In the contemporary era , geoeconomics often substitutes for direct conquest . Sanctions , export controls , and trade agreements function as instruments of statecraft . Economic coercion allows states to pursue strategic objectives . However , when economic measures fail , war is possible . <p> The competition between the US and China demonstrates how market access , technological supremacy , and supply chain control are central to modern rivalry . Tariffs , restrictions on semiconductor exports , and scrutiny of foreign investment reflect a shift from pure economic globalisation toward strategic economic nationalism . <p> Multipolar Competition in the 21st Century <p> The post -- Cold War period is marked by the relative dominance of the United States . However , the rapid rise of China , to a lesser extent , India , and the assertive re-emergence of Russia have ushered in a more multipolar environment . Trump 's tariff war against the rest of the world and its wanting to annex Canada and Greenland are attempts to reassert US dominance . <p> The conflict between Russia and Ukraine is not solely about territory , but reflects competing visions of political alignment , historical identity , and regional order , and underlying them all , the US desire to undermine Russia 's primacy as a major global energy supplier . Ukraine 's assertion of independent nationhood challenges Moscow 's conception of historical unity and strategic buffer zones against NATO 's relentless expansion in the last few decades . The result is a war that blends geopolitical calculation with deeply rooted identity claims . <p> In the Indo-Pacific , tensions between China and the United States revolve around maritime dominance , technological leadership , and the political status of Taiwan . Here , economic interdependence coexists with strategic rivalry . Semiconductor supply chains , artificial intelligence development , and naval presence in contested waters represent both economic and security stakes . <p> Influence of the US Dollar and Multinational Corporations <p> The 2003 invasion of Iraq is linked to the strategic importance of oil and the global financial system centred on the U.S. dollar . Because most international oil trade is priced in dollars -- often called the " petrodollar system " -- the stability of dollar-based energy markets is closely tied to U.S. economic power . Iraq possesses some of the largest oil reserves in the world , and control over oil production and pricing can influence global energy markets . Critics of the war argue that maintaining influence over major oil-producing regions helps sustain the dominance of the dollar and the global financial system built around it . Geopolitical interventions in oil-rich regions can be understood partly as attempts to preserve the economic architecture that supports U.S. financial and strategic influence . <p> A somewhat different but related dynamic can be seen in the political crisis in Venezuela , which holds the world 's largest proven oil reserves . Over the past two decades , Chinese state-linked companies and banks became deeply involved in Venezuela 's oil sector through loans , investments , and long-term supply agreements . China has extended billions of dollars in credit to Venezuela in exchange for future oil deliveries , making it one of the country 's most important economic partners . This growing Chinese presence in Venezuela 's energy industry has been viewed by some policymakers in Washington as a strategic challenge , especially because it expands China 's influence in a region traditionally considered within the United States ' sphere of influence . During Venezuela 's political crisis in 2019 , the United States recognized opposition leader Juan Guaid ? as interim president and imposed sanctions on the country 's state-owned oil company PDVSA , which is the main source of national revenue . <p> More recently , developments in Venezuela have continued to highlight the centrality of oil to geopolitical calculations . After intense U.S. pressure and sanctions targeting the oil sector , the United States intervened in the political situation and captured Venezuelan President Nicol ? s Maduro on 3 January 2026 , an action widely interpreted as linked to the country 's vast energy resources and the strategic importance of controlling their production and export . Some analysts argue that these actions reflect broader geopolitical competition over energy resources and market access , especially given that China has been a major importer of Venezuelan oil and a key financial partner . Control over such resources affects not only energy markets but also the broader balance of economic influence among global powers . <p> These cases illustrate a broader phenomenon described as crony capitalism , where political power and corporate interests become closely intertwined . In crony capitalist systems , major economic decisions -- such as access to natural resources , infrastructure contracts , or financial privileges -- are shaped not purely by market forces but by political relationships between governments and powerful corporations . In the global energy sector , this can manifest as close ties between governments , multinational oil companies , financial institutions , and political elites . Critics argue that such relationships can encourage foreign interventions , sanctions regimes , or political pressure aimed at securing favourable conditions for specific corporate or national economic interests . Conflicts over oil and energy resources frequently reflect not only geopolitical rivalry but also the interaction between state power and corporate influence in the global economy . <p> Oil has been the single most strategically important commodity in modern history . It reshaped the production of goods and services , transport , warfare , and became deeply intertwined with economic development , national power and geopolitics . From the early days of the oil rush in Pennsylvania in the latter half of the 19th Century to the rise of multinational oil companies and the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries ( OPEC ) , to the present day , oil has been a central force in global politics . <p> Oil had an intimate relationship with state power . By the late 19th Century , governments began to recognise that access to secure oil supplies was essential for military strength and industrial growth . In the early 20th century , oil replaced coal as the dominant strategic fuel , especially for navies and mechanised armies . This shift transformed energy from a commercial commodity into a national security imperative , linking oil fields and sea lanes to imperial ambition and global rivalry . <p> The balance of power shifted dramatically in the mid-20th Century as oil-producing countries in the Middle East renegotiated concessions and eventually nationalised assets . The formation of OPEC marked a turning point , giving producing nations collective leverage over global markets and demonstrating how resource control could translate into geopolitical influence . <p> After the 1973 Yom Kippur War between the Arabs and Israel , several Arab oil-producing states imposed an oil embargo on countries that supported Israel . The resulting oil supply shock caused soaring prices and economic recession . This event revealed the vulnerability of industrial economies to energy disruption and fundamentally reshaped energy policy , strategic reserves , and international relations . <p> Oil has been both a driver of economic development and prosperity and a source of conflict . It fuelled wars , underpinned alliances , empowered corporations and states , and repeatedly redrawn the geopolitical map . Control over energy resources -- more than ideology alone -- has determined the contours of modern global power . <p> Energy has played a critical role in wars . As First Lord of the Admiralty of the British Navy in 1911 , Churchill realised that war was imminent with Germany . He recognised the strategic need to switch the Royal Navy from coal to oil for greater speed and efficiency . Churchill then secured oil from new oil finds in Persia . In 1914 , he spearheaded an agreement where the British government purchased a 51% controlling stake in the Anglo-Persian Oil Company to secure a reliable supply for the Navy . <p> In 1942 , the German Army made a major , high-stakes effort to seize the Baku oil field to sustain their war effort . Despite intense fighting in the Caucasus and reaching as far as Grozny , they were eventually forced to retreat following the Stalingrad disaster . <p> Imperial Japan had no fossil fuel reserves of its own , so it invaded fossil fuel-rich areas until it was defeated in World War II . In 1931 , it colonised Manchuria in Northeast China for its rich coal fields . After bombing Pearl Harbour in 1941 , Japan invaded Indonesia , and not Singapore , as Indonesia had coal and gas . Toward the end of World War II , Japan experienced severe shortages of aviation fuel , leading it to use pine oil ( turpentine ) . Simultaneously , they formalised kamikaze tactics as a desperation measure to compensate for a lack of trained pilots , fuel for training , and to allow them to inflict damage with minimal oil resources . <p> Energy remains central to economic growth , geopolitical stability , and national security . Energy transitions are slow , complex , and shaped as much by politics and technology as by markets . <p> As energy demand surges in emerging economies -- especially in China and India -- energy security becomes a strategic concern . Access to oil and gas reserves , pipeline routes , and maritime chokepoints influences foreign policy decisions . Energy interdependence can both stabilise and destabilise relations : it creates mutual reliance , but also vulnerability to disruption . <p> In the last few decades , advances in hydraulic fracturing and horizontal drilling unlocked vast reserves of oil and gas previously considered uneconomical . This technological breakthrough transformed the United States from a declining producer into one of the world 's largest energy producers , reshaping global markets and reducing U.S. dependence on Middle Eastern imports . Innovation can dramatically alter geopolitical calculations . <p> The 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster in Japan triggered a global reassessment of nuclear energy policy , leading some countries to scale back or reconsider nuclear programs . Public perception , safety concerns , and political reaction can redirect the trajectory of energy development . <p> The global energy system is in transition . Fossil fuels will remain significant for decades , even as renewable energy expands . Energy security , technological innovation , environmental pressures , and geopolitical competition are deeply intertwined -- and managing this complex interplay will define the future of the world . <p> At its core , geopolitics is about the control , organisation , and transformation of energy , and its use in production systems that transform raw materials into finished goods and services . Military power rests on industrial capacity . Financial systems depend on energy flows . Technological supremacy requires global logistics networks . <p> The relative stability that followed the end of the Cold War -- characterised by economic globalisation , institutional multilateralism , and the predominance of the United States -- has given way to a far more fragmented and contested landscape . The rise of China , the assertive geopolitical posture of Russia and the war in Ukraine , the increasing strategic weight of India , and the growing economic rise of middle powers -- the EU , Japan , Canada , Australia , Brazil , South Africa and Indonesia , instability in the Middle East , tensions in the Indo-Pacific are deeply rooted in questions of energy access , industrial production , and market control . <p> The domains of competition now include not only land , sea , and air but also cyberspace , outer space , semiconductor fabrication facilities , rare earth processing plants , undersea cables , social media platforms , and artificial intelligence systems , all of which draw heavily from the use of energy , other raw materials and technology . <p> The present geopolitical condition can be described as competitive multipolarity embedded within persistent interdependence . Major powers compete intensely , but their economies remain intertwined . Regional conflicts erupt , yet global financial systems continue to function . States seek autonomy and resilience , but they can not fully detach from global networks without incurring severe costs . <p> The US and China : Energy , Production Systems , and the Structure of Rivalry <p> At the heart of contemporary geopolitics is the relationship between the United States and China . Although this rivalry is often framed as a military or ideological conflict , its more fundamental roots are in energy systems , industrial production , and control of key technological supply chains . Modern geopolitical power depends on the ability to mobilise large energy flows and transform them into industrial output , technological progress , and military strength . <p> China 's rise over the past four decades has been driven by an extraordinary expansion of industrial production powered primarily by coal-based electricity and supported by integration into global markets . Large-scale energy availability enabled China to become the world 's manufacturing centre . Export-oriented industrialisation allowed China to accumulate capital , build infrastructure , and develop technological capabilities . Over time , the country moved up the industrial value chain from labour-intensive manufacturing toward advanced sectors such as electronics , telecommunications equipment , renewable energy technologies , and digital platforms . Today , China is the largest producer of solar panels , wind turbines , and electric vehicles , and it dominates the processing of rare earth minerals essential to modern electronics and energy technologies . <p> This transformation illustrates a central principle of geopolitical economy : industrial power follows energy availability . China 's massive coal reserves , combined with the rapid expansion of electricity generation capacity , provided the energetic foundation for its manufacturing expansion . At the same time , China became increasingly dependent on imported oil and natural gas to sustain transport systems , petrochemicals , and industrial activity . As a result , securing energy supplies became a major strategic priority . Long-term supply contracts , overseas investments in energy infrastructure , and maritime security policies reflect the importance of ensuring continuous energy flows to the Chinese economy . <p> The United States , by contrast , developed as an industrial superpower during the 20th Century based on abundant domestic fossil fuel resources , technological innovation , and large-scale industrial production . Although the United States experienced partial deindustrialisation in certain manufacturing sectors during the late 20th and early 21st centuries , it retains leadership in advanced technological fields such as semiconductor design , aerospace , artificial intelligence research , and digital platforms . Its financial system , anchored by the global role of the dollar , also remains central to global markets . <p> Energy continues to play a critical role in sustaining American geopolitical influence . The rapid expansion of shale oil and gas production transformed the United States into one of the world 's largest energy producers and exporters . In particular , the growth of liquefied natural gas exports has strengthened ties between the United States and energy-importing allies in Europe and Asia , providing an alternative to supplies from other major producers . Energy exports thus function not only as commercial transactions but also as instruments of geopolitical influence . <p> The rivalry between the United States and China is about control over critical segments of the global production system . Leadership in battery manufacturing , semiconductor fabrication , artificial intelligence infrastructure , telecommunications equipment , and aerospace technologies translates into both economic productivity and military capability . These sectors depend on complex supply chains linking energy extraction , mineral processing , industrial manufacturing , and technological innovation . <p> Unlike the Cold War confrontation between the United States and the Soviet Union , the U.S. -- China relationship is characterised by profound economic interdependence . Global supply chains connect firms and industries across both economies . Multinational corporations manufacture products in China for global markets while relying on American technology , financial services , and consumer demand . Financial markets remain deeply integrated . This interdependence complicates strategic competition , because aggressive decoupling would impose high costs on both sides and disrupt global production networks . <p> At the same time , governments in both countries increasingly view supply chain resilience and technological autonomy as strategic priorities . The United States has introduced export controls restricting China 's access to advanced semiconductor technologies and chip-manufacturing equipment . China has responded by investing heavily in domestic semiconductor production , artificial intelligence development , and research capacity in emerging technologies such as quantum computing and advanced telecommunications infrastructure . <p> Energy systems intersect with this competition in multiple ways . The transition toward renewable energy technologies -- solar panels , wind turbines , batteries , and electric vehicles -- creates new arenas of industrial rivalry . China 's dominance in renewable energy manufacturing reflects large-scale investment , integrated supply chains , and control over key mineral processing industries . The United States and its allies are attempting to expand domestic manufacturing capacity and diversify supply chains to reduce dependence on Chinese production . <p> Geography also plays a role in shaping the rivalry . Maritime trade routes in the Indo-Pacific carry a large share of global energy and commodity flows . China 's dependence on imported oil transported through narrow sea lanes heightens its concern with maritime security and regional stability . Meanwhile , American alliances and naval presence in the region reinforce its role as a guarantor of maritime trade routes . <p> The Taiwan Strait represents the most dangerous flashpoint within this broader rivalry . The strategic importance of Taiwan extends far beyond politics . Taiwan hosts some of the world 's most advanced semiconductor manufacturing facilities , producing chips essential for global electronics , computing systems , artificial intelligence , and advanced weapons platforms . A disruption to Taiwan 's semiconductor production would ripple across the entire global economy , affecting industries from automobiles and telecommunications to aerospace and defence . The island , therefore , represents a critical node in the global production system , making any conflict there a potential economic shock of unprecedented scale . <p> Ultimately , the rivalry between the United States and China is best understood as a contest over the organisation of the global energy -- industrial system . Energy availability enables industrial production ; industrial capacity enables technological innovation ; and technological leadership confers economic and military advantage . Control over supply chains , production technologies , and energy infrastructure , therefore , becomes a central objective of state strategy . <p> The outcome of this rivalry will help determine the structure of the global economy in the coming decades . Whether the world moves toward deeper fragmentation of production networks or manages to maintain a degree of cooperative interdependence will depend largely on how the United States and China navigate this complex interplay of energy systems , industrial power , and geopolitical ambition . <p> Russia , Ukraine , and the Energy Restructuring of Europe <p> Russia 's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 represents one of the clearest demonstrations of how energy systems and markets can become instruments of geopolitical power . In the decades preceding the conflict , Russia had become one of the world 's largest exporters of oil , natural gas , and coal , and a particularly dominant supplier of piped gas to Europe . This energy relationship formed a central pillar of the economic interdependence between Russia and Europe . When the war began , the disruption of these flows triggered one of the largest reorganisations of global energy markets in recent history . <p> Before 2022 , many European countries depended heavily on Russian natural gas transported through an extensive network of pipelines crossing Eastern Europe and the Baltic region . Russian energy exports not only generated large revenues for the Russian state but also gave Moscow considerable geopolitical leverage over energy-importing countries . The invasion of Ukraine and the subsequent sanctions imposed by Western governments fundamentally altered this relationship . Sanctions targeted Russian financial institutions , restricted access to advanced technology , and imposed limits on energy trade . In response , Europe moved rapidly to reduce dependence on Russian pipeline gas . <p> The adjustment required a dramatic restructuring of Europe 's energy supply system . Liquefied natural gas ( LNG ) imports increased sharply as European states turned to alternative suppliers , including shipments from the United States and other exporting countries . New LNG terminals were constructed or expanded , and pipeline infrastructure was reconfigured to enable energy flows from different sources . At the same time , European governments accelerated the deployment of renewable energy technologies such as wind and solar power to reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels . Nuclear energy , previously in decline in several countries , re-emerged in policy debates as governments reconsidered the importance of stable , domestically produced electricity . <p> These changes reveal how energy systems shape geopolitical relationships . Russia 's ability to supply large quantities of natural gas had previously created economic interdependence that some policymakers believed would stabilise political relations . The war demonstrated the opposite possibility : energy dependence can create vulnerability when political relations deteriorate . By reducing its reliance on Russian gas , Europe sought to transform that vulnerability into a more diversified and resilient energy structure . <p> For Russia , the consequences were equally significant . Sanctions and declining European demand forced the country to redirect energy exports toward alternative markets , particularly in Asia . Oil shipments were rerouted through longer maritime routes , and new trade relationships developed with countries willing to purchase discounted Russian energy . This redirection of trade flows altered the geography of global energy markets and strengthened Russia 's economic ties with countries outside the Western sanctions regime , including China and other emerging economies . <p> The war also demonstrated how energy markets transmit geopolitical shocks across the global economy . Disruptions to Russian oil and gas exports caused price volatility in international energy markets . Because energy is a key input in transportation , manufacturing , and agriculture , rising energy prices cascaded through supply chains . Fertiliser production , which depends heavily on natural gas , became more expensive , contributing to higher food prices . Grain exports from the Black Sea region were also disrupted by the conflict , further intensifying pressure on the global food market . <p> Beyond its economic consequences , the war has reshaped Europe 's strategic landscape . The conflict has evolved into a prolonged war of attrition characterised by extensive use of drones , long-range missiles , trench fortifications , and cyber operations . Western governments have provided substantial military and financial assistance to Ukraine while maintaining economic sanctions against Russia . These developments have reinforced the importance of collective defence arrangements within the NATO alliance , which has expanded its membership and strengthened its presence along its eastern frontier . <p> European defence spending has increased significantly as governments reassess security risks in light of the war . The concept of European strategic autonomy -- once discussed primarily in terms of diplomatic independence -- has increasingly been linked to industrial capacity , technological capability , and energy security . Energy infrastructure , supply chains for military equipment , and domestic industrial production are now viewed as essential components of national and regional security . <p> Energy politics , therefore , sits at the centre of the conflict 's geopolitical consequences . The disruption of Russian energy exports forced Europe to reconsider its energy strategy , accelerate the transition toward renewable energy sources , and diversify supply chains . At the same time , Russia has attempted to reposition itself within global markets by strengthening economic relationships with non-Western partners and by adapting export routes to circumvent sanctions . <p> The broader lesson of the Russia -- Ukraine war is that energy markets are not merely economic mechanisms but strategic systems capable of transmitting geopolitical power . Control over energy resources and transportation routes can generate political leverage , while dependence on external suppliers can create strategic vulnerability . When conflicts disrupt these systems , the effects extend far beyond the battlefield , influencing inflation , trade flows , industrial production , and financial stability across the global economy . <p> In this sense , the war represents not only a military confrontation but also a major episode in the ongoing reorganisation of the global energy system . Europe 's shift away from Russian energy , Russia 's reorientation toward alternative markets , and the acceleration of renewable energy deployment all reflect the ways in which geopolitical conflict can reshape the structure of global energy production and trade . <p> The conflict demonstrates that energy remains one of the most powerful forces shaping international politics , linking war , markets , and industrial systems into a single geopolitical dynamic . <p> The Middle East : Energy , Conflict , and Strategic Realignment <p> The Middle East occupies a central position in global geopolitics largely because of its role in the world 's energy system . The region contains some of the largest proven reserves of oil and natural gas and has long functioned as a primary supplier of energy to global markets . Revenues from hydrocarbon exports finance state budgets , sovereign wealth funds , infrastructure development , and geopolitical initiatives across the region . As a result , political stability in the Middle East is closely linked to the functioning of international energy markets . Conflicts in the region carry consequences far beyond local politics , affecting global trade flows , commodity prices , and economic stability . <p> Oil production decisions by major exporters such as Saudi Arabia continue to influence global energy prices . Through coordination within production alliances , regional producers can adjust supply levels and thereby affect market conditions . This capacity gives energy-exporting states significant geopolitical leverage , as fluctuations in oil prices influence inflation , government revenues , and economic performance across the world . In this sense , the Middle East functions as one of the key nodes in the global energy system . <p> At the same time , the region remains one of the most politically volatile areas of the international system . The ongoing conflict between Israel and Hamas has generated severe humanitarian consequences and heightened fears of wider regional escalation involving Iran and other actors . While the immediate conflict is geographically concentrated , its effects extend far beyond the battlefield because the Middle East lies astride some of the most important energy transportation routes in the world . <p> Shipping disruptions in the Red Sea have demonstrated how even localised conflict can influence global markets . A significant portion of global trade -- including energy shipments -- passes through maritime corridors connecting the Persian Gulf , the Red Sea , and the Mediterranean . When insecurity increases along these routes , shipping costs rise and global supply chains experience delays . Energy markets are particularly sensitive to such disruptions because oil and liquefied natural gas shipments depend heavily on secure maritime transportation . Consequently , regional conflicts can quickly translate into volatility in global commodity prices . <p> The economic and political importance of hydrocarbons has also shaped the strategies of the region 's major states . Gulf countries such as Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have accumulated enormous financial resources through decades of oil exports . These revenues are increasingly being used to finance long-term economic diversification strategies designed to prepare for a future in which fossil fuel demand may gradually decline . Investments in renewable energy , logistics infrastructure , digital technology , tourism , and global financial assets are intended to transform hydrocarbon wealth into broader economic investments . <p> Energy-exporting states are increasingly pursuing strategies of strategic hedging in response to the emerging multipolar order . While maintaining long-standing security relationships with the United States , many Gulf states are expanding economic and technological partnerships with China and other emerging powers . This diversification of external relationships reflects a pragmatic approach to geopolitics in which economic opportunities and market access take precedence over rigid ideological alignments . <p> Tensions involving Israel , Iran , and various non-state actors create persistent uncertainty that can affect market confidence and investment decisions . Energy infrastructure , shipping routes , and production facilities are all potential targets in regional confrontations . Even when direct damage to energy production is limited , the perception of risk can influence global oil prices and insurance costs for maritime transport . <p> Despite these challenges , many governments in the region are attempting to reposition their economies for the long term . Renewable energy projects are increasingly prominent in national development plans . These initiatives reflect recognition that the global energy transition may gradually reshape the geopolitical importance of fossil fuels . By investing in new energy technologies and diversified industries , Gulf states hope to remain central players in the evolving global energy system . <p> The geopolitics of the Middle East is part of the broader global effort to control energy resources , manage energy markets , and adapt national economies to an evolving energy landscape . The region remains both a major supplier of energy to the world and a focal point where the interaction of energy , finance , and geopolitics continues to shape the structure of the global economy . <p> Other Wars after World War II <p> Many wars have been fought since the end of World War II . A list of major inter-state wars , without comment , is given below : <p> The technological revolution reshapes geopolitics at every level . Artificial intelligence accelerates economic productivity while introducing military applications such as autonomous weapons , advanced surveillance , and cyberattacks that target infrastructure , elections , and financial systems . Space has become militarised , with satellites underpinning communication , navigation , and reconnaissance . <p> Control over data , algorithms , and digital infrastructure is as consequential as control over territory . Semiconductor fabrication plants become strategic assets . Undersea cables become vulnerable . Social media platforms become arenas of influence operations . <p> Climate Change , Energy Transition , and the Reorganisation of Global Production <p> Climate change is increasingly reshaping geopolitics not only through environmental impacts but also through the transformation of energy systems and industrial production . Rising temperatures , extreme weather events , and ecological stress act as multipliers of existing geopolitical tensions . Floods , droughts , and heatwaves damage infrastructure , disrupt transportation networks , and interrupt industrial supply chains . Agricultural production becomes more volatile , affecting global food markets and increasing the risk of political instability in vulnerable regions . Climate-driven migration further intensifies social and political pressures , particularly in regions already facing economic or environmental stress . <p> Beyond these immediate effects , climate change is catalysing a profound restructuring of global energy systems and industrial production . Efforts to limit greenhouse gas emissions require a transition away from fossil fuels toward electrification , renewable energy , and new industrial processes . This transformation is forcing governments and industries to reconfigure the technological and infrastructural foundations of modern economies . Electrification of transportation , large-scale deployment of renewable electricity , decarbonisation of heavy industries such as steel and cement , and modernisation of electricity grids all demand massive investment in new technologies and infrastructure . <p> Because these transformations affect the core of industrial production , climate policy has effectively become a form of industrial policy . Governments are competing to develop domestic manufacturing capacity in sectors such as solar panels , wind turbines , batteries , electric vehicles , and advanced energy storage systems . Countries that establish leadership in these technologies gain not only environmental benefits but also economic advantages through exports , technological innovation , and industrial employment . As a result , the transition to low-carbon energy systems is generating a new arena of geopolitical competition centred on control of emerging green industries . <p> At the same time , the energy transition is altering patterns of resource dependence . Reducing reliance on fossil fuels diminishes the strategic importance of traditional oil and gas exporters , but it simultaneously increases demand for minerals essential to renewable technologies . Lithium , cobalt , nickel , copper , and rare earth elements are required for batteries , electric motors , wind turbines , and other components of the low-carbon economy . This shift transfers geopolitical attention from hydrocarbon reserves to mineral deposits and the industrial processes required to refine and manufacture these materials into usable technologies . <p> Consequently , the geopolitical hierarchy of energy resources is being reorganised rather than eliminated . Countries that control critical mineral supplies or dominate processing and manufacturing capabilities gain strategic influence in the emerging energy system . The transition to renewable energy , therefore , does not remove the geopolitical significance of energy resources ; instead , it relocates it within new supply chains and industrial sectors . <p> Climate change also affects geopolitical dynamics through its impact on geography . Melting Arctic ice is gradually opening new maritime routes and increasing access to previously inaccessible natural resources . This development intensifies strategic competition among Arctic states seeking to secure shipping lanes , resource claims , and military presence in the region . At the same time , rising sea levels and extreme weather events threaten coastal infrastructure and densely populated urban regions , creating new security challenges for many countries . <p> Another dimension of climate geopolitics lies in disputes over responsibility and financial support . Developing countries , which often face the most severe climate impacts despite contributing relatively little to historical emissions , are demanding greater financial assistance for adaptation and mitigation efforts . Negotiations over climate finance , technology transfer , and development pathways have therefore become major points of contention between industrialised and developing nations . These debates reflect deeper questions about economic equity and the distribution of the costs associated with global decarbonisation . <p> The transformation of energy systems also interacts with global production networks . Manufacturing supply chains must adapt to new materials , technologies , and energy sources . Industries that depend heavily on fossil fuels are being pressured to adopt alternative energy inputs and more efficient production processes . In sectors such as steel , cement , chemicals , and transportation , the development of low-carbon production methods requires extensive technological innovation and capital investment . <p> As a result , the transition to a low-carbon economy is reshaping global industrial geography . Countries capable of combining technological innovation , access to critical minerals , and large-scale manufacturing capacity are likely to become leaders in the emerging energy system . Others may struggle to adapt if they remain dependent on fossil fuel exports or lack the industrial infrastructure required to participate in new energy technologies . <p> In this sense , climate change is not merely an environmental issue but a catalyst for a broader reconfiguration of economic and geopolitical power . The shift from fossil fuel -- based energy systems to renewable and electrified technologies is reorganising supply chains , altering patterns of resource dependence , and reshaping global production networks . Countries that successfully adapt their industrial systems to this new energy landscape will gain economic and strategic advantages , while those that fail to do so may find themselves marginalised in the emerging global order . <p> ENERGY AND NON-RENEWABLE MINERALS CRISES <p> Peak oil refers to the point at which the production of oil reaches its maximum rate and then begins to decline . Oil production follows a bell-shaped curve : production rises as new fields are discovered and developed , peaks when roughly half the resource has been extracted , and then declines as remaining reserves become harder and more expensive to exploit . Oil production will become increasingly difficult and costly after half of the original oil reserves are extracted . This can lead to economic and geopolitical stresses because modern transport , agriculture , and industry depend heavily on petroleum . <p> Reliable statistics for shale oil and gas are not available . At current rates of use of fossil fuels and uranium ore , fossil fuels and uranium ore will be exhausted by the end of this century . <p> Current energy use of 15 Gtoe is growing at 2% pa . If this growth rate continues , the world will require 109 Gtoe in 100 years from now and 787 Gtoe , 200 years from now . Fossil fuels are highly energy-dense , easily transportable , and capable of providing continuous power . Where will the energy requirement come from 100-200 years hence ? Solar and wind energies can not fully replace current fossil fuel consumption . <p> Closely related to peak oil is the idea of peak materials . About 4-5 billion tonnes of minerals and metals such as iron , copper , lithium , nickel , rare earth elements , and phosphorus are extracted annually , and extraction is growing by 2-3% pa . Over time , mining must shift to lower-grade ores that require more energy , water , and capital to process . This leads to declining returns from extraction . Since many modern technologies -- including renewable energy systems -- depend on large quantities of these materials , peak materials could impose constraints on future industrial development . <p> Another concept that highlights these limitations is the energy cliff , which is closely related to the idea of EROEI . High-quality energy sources , such as early oil fields , produced very large returns -- sometimes more than 50 units of energy for every unit invested . As resources become harder to extract , the energy required for extraction rises , and the net energy available to society declines . The " energy cliff " refers to the steep drop in net usable energy that occurs when EROEI falls below 5 . Even if gross energy production remains high , the portion of energy available to run the rest of the economy shrinks rapidly once extraction costs increase . <p> Together , these concepts suggest that modern societies face significant challenges in maintaining the large energy surpluses that support complex industrial systems . Peak oil and peak materials indicate potential limits to resource extraction , while the energy cliff highlights the importance of net energy rather than total energy production . Renewable energy technologies may help mitigate these constraints , but their ability to fully replace fossil fuels depends on overcoming technical , economic , and material limitations . Understanding these dynamics is essential for evaluating the long-term sustainability of industrial civilisation . <p> ENERGY DECLINE COLLAPSED PAST CIVILISATIONS ; WILL IT HAPPEN AGAIN ? <p> Many great civilisations of the past declined or disappeared not as a result of invasion , moral decline , or natural disasters , but because they could not obtain enough energy and resources to sustain themselves . Human societies grow more complex over time because complexity helps them solve problems . As populations increase and societies expand , new challenges arise -- such as defending territory , managing agriculture , organising trade , and resolving conflicts . To deal with these challenges , societies develop institutions and systems that increase their organisational complexity . Governments become more elaborate , bureaucracies grow , armies are formed , and infrastructure such as roads , irrigation systems , and public buildings is constructed . These developments allow societies to manage large populations and territories more effectively . <p> However , increasing complexity always requires energy and resources . Complex societies must feed administrators and soldiers , maintain infrastructure , support specialised workers , and sustain urban populations that do not directly produce food . All of this depends on the ability to extract energy from the environment through agriculture , forestry , mining , and other economic activities . Every civilisation rests upon an underlying energy base that supports its institutions and structures . <p> In the early stages of a civilisation 's development , energy resources are usually abundant and relatively easy to exploit . Agricultural land is fertile , forests are plentiful , and mineral deposits are rich . Under these conditions , societies can increase production with relatively little effort . Expansion of farmland , irrigation systems , and trade networks produces large gains in productivity . The resulting energy surplus supports growing populations , expanding cities , and increasingly complex social systems . <p> Over time , however , the most accessible and productive resources tend to be used up . Agricultural land becomes less fertile , forests are depleted , and mineral deposits become harder to extract . To maintain the same level of production , societies must invest more labour , resources , and organisation . In other words , the energy return from resource extraction begins to decline . This process is described as " declining marginal returns to complexity . " The solutions that societies develop to solve problems -- such as larger bureaucracies , more extensive infrastructure , or more powerful armies -- become increasingly costly relative to the benefits they provide . <p> Eventually , a point may be reached where the costs of maintaining a complex society exceed the benefits . When the available energy surplus is no longer sufficient to support existing institutions , societies become vulnerable to disruption . At this stage , external shocks such as invasion , drought , or political instability can trigger a rapid decline . This process leads to " collapse . " Importantly , collapse does not necessarily mean the disappearance of a population . Rather , it means a sudden reduction in social complexity . <p> When complex systems can no longer be sustained , societies simplify . Governments break down or fragment into smaller political units . Large cities may be abandoned . Long-distance trade networks decline . Specialised occupations disappear as communities return to more local forms of production . Population levels often fall , and economic activity becomes more localised . In essence , the society reorganises itself into a simpler structure that requires less energy to maintain . <p> An important historical example is the Roman Empire . At its height , the Roman Empire controlled a vast territory stretching across Europe , North Africa , and the Middle East . The empire 's early expansion brought enormous wealth in the form of agricultural land , minerals , tribute , and slaves . These resources provided the energy surplus that supported Rome 's complex institutions -- its army , administrative bureaucracy , road network , and urban infrastructure . <p> However , once Rome stopped expanding in the 2nd Century CE , it could no longer rely on new conquests to supply additional resources . At the same time , the costs of maintaining the empire continued to rise . Defending long frontiers required large standing armies , while taxes and administrative systems became increasingly burdensome . Agricultural productivity stagnated , and mining operations became less profitable as high-quality deposits were exhausted . As the energy surplus declined , the empire found it increasingly difficult to sustain its complex political and military structures . In the 5th Century CE , the western part of the empire collapsed , fragmenting into smaller political units and experiencing a sharp decline in urban life and long-distance trade . <p> Another example is the collapse of the Mayan civilisation in Central America during the 8th and 9th centuries . The Mayans built impressive cities and monuments supported by intensive agricultural systems . As populations grew , farming became more demanding , requiring terraces , irrigation systems , and other complex techniques to maintain food production . Over time , environmental pressures such as deforestation , soil degradation , and drought reduced agricultural productivity . When food production declined , the elaborate political and religious structures that governed Mayan cities could no longer be sustained . Many major urban centres were abandoned , and the civilisation fragmented into smaller communities . <p> In Chaco Canyon in North America , complex settlement systems developed in environments with limited natural resources . These societies relied on trade networks and careful management of agricultural land . Over time , environmental degradation and climatic changes reduced productivity , making it increasingly difficult to maintain the complex social and economic systems that had developed . Eventually , the large settlements were abandoned , and the population dispersed into smaller communities . <p> These societies did not voluntarily choose to simplify . Complex institutions existed because they solved important problems . Governments maintain armies to defend against enemies , bureaucracies to manage taxation and administration , and infrastructure to support economic activity . Even when these systems become expensive , abandoning them creates new risks . As a result , societies tend to continue investing in complexity even when the returns are declining . Collapse occurs when the costs become unsustainable , and the system can no longer function . <p> Past civilisational collapses have implications for the modern world . Industrial civilisation tapped the vast deposits of fossil fuels and invented technologies to use them , which supported the development of modern economies , global transportation systems , and large nation-states . The enormous energy surplus created by fossil fuels made it possible to sustain unprecedented levels of complexity , including advanced technology , large cities , global trade networks , and sophisticated governments . <p> If high-quality energy resources decline or become more difficult to obtain , societies could once again face declining returns on complexity . Maintaining modern infrastructures , technological systems , and global institutions requires vast amounts of energy . If the energy base supporting these systems weakens , the pressures that contributed to past collapses could reappear . Behind every complex society lies a foundation of energy and resources -- and that is when this foundation weakens , even the most powerful civilisations can decline . <p> POSTSCRIPT <p> Recent events quite clearly indicate how the political games that the US is playing are very heavily influenced by its compulsion to control energy and financial sources and restrict its rivals in the marketplace . <p> There was a general perception that international water wars would begin in a decade or two hence , followed by energy wars . But recent events in Venezuela and Iran indicate that energy wars have begun . Though the Russian invasion of Ukraine is seen as one being waged to retain Russian territorial security , the production and sale of Russian fossil fuels are interwoven in this conflict . <p> Soon after Trump became the president of the United States of America , he announced his desire to make Canada the 51st state of the USA and annex or buy Greenland . Canada has abundant fossil fuels , uranium and rare earth reserves . Moreover , Canada and the USA have deeply intertwined supply chains and markets . Greenland is important to the USA not just from a strategic point of view , but also because it has rare earth reserves . <p> Trump now has a say in Venezuela 's oil <p> The USA now has considerable influence over Venezuela 's oil , the largest proven deposits in the world , and its considerable gas deposits . And US companies can now make profits by extracting and selling Venezuelan oil , which they previously could not . <p> After Maduro was kidnapped , acting President Delcy Rodr ? guez moved away from strict state control of the country 's oil . Private companies can now take full operational control of production and sales , paving the way for American oil companies to invest in Venezuelan oil and make profits . The new law allows disputes to be settled through international arbitration , rather than by Venezuela 's courts . Fiscal terms have been sweetened with caps on royalties and taxes . <p> The US Treasury simultaneously issued a general license that eases sanctions , allowing US companies to export , store , and trade Venezuelan oil , but payments must generally flow through US-controlled accounts , and contracts must be governed by US law . <p> Trump wants a say in Iran 's fossil fuels control <p> Iran is a country with the third-largest oil reserves and the second-largest gas reserves in the world , allegedly to make Iran curtail its nuclear programme . Iran 's oil and gas resources are under state control . As a result of heavy international sanctions , primarily led by the US , Iran sells 80-90% of its oil to China , and the balance to India , Japan and South Korea . <p> The sanctions target Iran 's petroleum , petrochemical , and oil product sales , cut Iranian banks off from the global financial system , notably the SWIFT messaging system , making international transactions extremely difficult , target the " shadow fleet " of tankers and their insurers , aiming to choke off shipping routes . The US Treasury regularly updates a " Specially Designated Nationals " list consisting of hundreds of individuals and firms , whose assets it freezes , and prohibits US transactions if these individuals and firms are linked to Iran 's energy and weapons trade . <p> The sanctions have impacted Iran 's economy and its role in the global energy markets profoundly . They have severely restricted access to foreign technology , investment , and financing , hindering the maintenance and growth of Iran 's oil fields . Experts warn this is causing a long-term , " slow-burning negative spiral " in Iran 's oil sector . Domestically , the sanctions have contributed to severe inflation , currency devaluation , and economic hardship for ordinary Iranians . <p> While Iran 's resource wealth is immense , its ability to fully leverage its oil and gas is crippled by international pressure , forcing it into a dependent relationship with China and stunting the long-term health of its energy industry . <p> Trump is now waging war on Iran . And Iran has shut the Hormuz Straits , through which about 20% of the world 's oil and gas moves . Brent oil prices shot up from the US$ 65-70/bbl range in late February to a peak of US$ 120/bbl on 9 March before falling to US$ 104/bbl by 16 March after the G7 signalled it is ready to release emergency oil reserves to stabilise the market . Oil prices are expected to remain volatile . <p> The ongoing war with Iran is sending shockwaves through the global economy . The impact varies dramatically : energy-importing nations face severe economic strain , while some energy exporters stand to gain . The short-term impacts of the war may see an inflationary trend in the global economy ( every 10% oil price rise adds 0.4% to global inflation ) , shipping costs and insurance premiums will rise as vessels are diverted from the Suez Canal , fertilizer prices will spike due to supply disruptions , raising costs for farmers globally and threatening to push food prices higher , especially in low-income countries . <p> If the war continues for a prolonged period , the long-term impacts will cause high energy prices to become the new normal . Global supply chains will permanently reroute , increasing costs . Permanent shifts in trade routes could reduce efficiency . Countries heavily reliant on Gulf imports may face structural trade deficits . Investment in alternative energy sources may accelerate . There is a risk of stagflation ( low growth + high inflation ) setting in . A stronger US dollar and tighter global financial conditions make it harder for emerging markets to borrow . Prolonged high fertiliser costs may lead to reduced crop yields and chronic food shortages in the most vulnerable nations . <p> Energy importers ( most of Europe , India , China , Japan , South Korea , Pakistan ) will be the losers and energy exporters outside the war zone ( Russia , Norway , Canada , and some Latin American &amp; African nations ) will benefit from higher oil prices . <p> The short term impact on India will increase India 's oil import bill by US$ 14-16 billion for a rise of every US$ 10/bbl . India imports 85% of its oil , 68% of its LNG , and 47% of its LPG . Qatar has already paused LNG deliveries . This will widen the Current Account Deficit and weaken the Rupee against the US Dollar . <p> Some of the immediate impacts on the Indian industry will include airline travel becoming costlier as aviation turbine fuel prices will increase , input costs for fertilisers , petrochemicals , and textiles will surge , rough cut diamonds from West Asia will decrease , and export of ceramic tiles to the same region will diminish . About 9 million Indian diaspora in the Gulf , who send back over US$ 80 billion annually ( approximately 2% of GDP ) , face job uncertainty . <p> India 's muted response , bordering on silence , to Israel and the US aggression on Iran and Israel 's genocide in Gaza , is indicative of the Indian government 's alignment vis- ? -vis Israel and the US . The US " permission " to India to increase Russian crude is meant to stabilise crude oil prices and is not a favour to India . The opposition to India 's position on the events unfolding in the Middle East from within India has been feeble . <p> By targeting enemy oil facilities , the US and Iran have weaponised fossil fuels . Trump has gone further than wanting regime change in Iran . He wants a say in the choice of Iran 's next leader , i.e. , the US wishes to control Iran 's energy resources . <p> In its attempt to retain its status as the prima donna in the world , the US has moved the world from a rule-of-law state to a law-of-the-jungle state . The US wants to become the sole imperial power in the world , a concept it was opposed to in the 20th Century . Will China , Russia and the Middle Power countries like India and the EU allow the US to do this ? <p> AGENDA THAT WORKING AND VULNERABLE POPULATIONS SHOULD ASK FOR <p> Sustainability : Developed nations must pledge to become net carbon negative in consumption emissions by 2035-40 to create space for developing nations to fully decarbonise by 2045-50 . <p> Note : Decarbonisation must focus primarily on : a ) Mitigation focussed on the reduction of consumption levels in the Global North , and supply-side management , leaving &gt;90% of the remaining fossil fuel reserves in the ground ; b ) Sequestration focussed on Nature-based Solutions that centre climate and social justice . In addition , decarbonisation strategies must eschew failed , untested , hypothetical market-based solutions and techno-fixes . Through these means , gross global consumption should be reduced to sustainable levels , the measure for which should be a quantifiable justice-centric sustainability index . <p> Environmental justice:a ) Responsibility for loss &amp; damage : Nations/regions should take responsibility for climate change impacts attributable to them -- displacement , property loss , etc -- in proportion to their cumulative emissions ( emissions from 1750-to date ) ; b ) Sharing benefits and risks equitably : Engineering and administrative controls should be put into place ( e.g. , global warming mitigative and adaptive measures , facilitating population migration where risk becomes high ) such that all people of the world face roughly the same degree of risk from the impacts of GHG emissions ; and the wealth created by the use of fossil fuels are distributed equally to all people of the world . <p> Equity : The ratio of the maximum income consumption for all people in the world should be5 <p> Decentralisation , democratic , transparent governance : Governance should be decentralised and democratic ; all governance information should be in the public domain . <p> In short , we have power down and bring in a regime of energy equity . Whether we will have the wisdom to do this before warming exceeds a 2 oC temperature rise , before there is an energy collapse , and before the inequity tips society over , is moot . <p> Acknowledgements <p> I am very grateful to Nandan Nawn , Sudhindra Seshadri and V Janardan for reading this paper and offering valuable suggestions to improve it . @@135495337 <h> Humanity at the Crossroads From War Consciousness to Peace Civilization <p> Lt Gen Narendra Kotwal ( R ) narendrakotwal@gmail.com Humanity today stands at a profound crossroads . On one hand , we inhabit an era of extraordinary scientific achievement , unprecedented connectivity , and remarkable technological advancement . We can communicate across continents in seconds , decode the human genome , and explore the depths of space . Yet on the other hand , the world remains troubled by an unsettling paradox : despite such progress , armed conflicts continue to scar our planet . As of early 2026 , more than 130 armed conflicts remain active across the globe , with high-intensity wars causing devastating loss of life in regions such as Ukraine , Sudan , Gaza , Myanmar , and parts of Africa . In addition , rising geopolitical tensions in the Middle East , including conflicts involving Iran , Israel , and global powers , threaten to widen the circle of instability . Millions of people have been displaced , families separated , cities destroyed , and generations traumatized . These tragedies raise a deeply unsettling @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ moral teachings , does humanity still engage in war ? To understand this dilemma , one must look beyond immediate political events and examine deeper layers of human nature , history , and social organization . Anthropologists and evolutionary biologists often point out that the human brain evolved in environments where small groups competed for survival . Early human tribes struggled over food , territory , and security . These evolutionary pressures shaped instincts that still influence modern behaviour : a tendency to form strong " in-groups " while perceiving outsiders with suspicion , fear , or hostility . Although our societies have grown vastly more complex , these ancient psychological patterns remain embedded in human consciousness . When political narratives exploit these instincts by framing conflicts in terms of identity , nationalism , religion , or perceived threats , large populations can be mobilized for confrontation . However , biological instincts alone can not explain modern wars . Contemporary conflicts are also deeply intertwined with economics , geopolitics , and power structures . Control over strategic resources such as oil , minerals , trade routes , and technological dominance @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ worth hundreds of billions of dollars annually , further complicates the picture by creating economic incentives that can perpetuate cycles of militarization . In such an environment , war sometimes becomes not merely a tragic outcome but a mechanism embedded within broader systems of power , influence , and profit . Equally important is the psychological dimension of leadership and mass perception . History repeatedly demonstrates that collective fear , pride , humiliation , or ideological fervour can fuel conflict . Leaders may project strength to maintain domestic legitimacy or strategic advantage , while propaganda and media narratives often shape public opinion by portraying adversaries as existential threats . When people are convinced that their nation , culture , or survival is under attack , they may support war even when its human cost is immense . Perhaps the most painful paradox of warfare lies in the human stories behind it . Soldiers who fight on battlefields are often young men and women who leave behind parents , spouses , and children . They carry the hopes and fears of families who wish only for their safe return . Yet @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by political or strategic elites far removed from the front lines . Throughout history , many leaders who advocate military action do not personally experience its physical dangers . This imbalance between decision-making power and human sacrifice has long troubled philosophers , ethicists , and ordinary citizens alike . Despite these grim realities , humanity has never lacked voices calling for peace . Ancient civilizations recognized the destructive consequences of unchecked ambition and hatred . In the Indian philosophical tradition , the concept of " Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam " -the world as one family-expresses the idea that all human beings share a fundamental unity . This perspective encourages individuals and societies to see beyond narrow identities and recognize the interconnectedness of life . Similarly , teachings from the Bhagavad Gita and other spiritual texts emphasize mastery over inner forces such as greed , anger , and ego . According to this wisdom , the true battles humanity must confront are not merely external conflicts but internal struggles against ignorance and destructive impulses . Modern science , interestingly , increasingly echoes these ancient insights . Neuroscience reveals that the human brain is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and understand the emotions of others . Evolutionary biology and game theory suggest that cooperation and trust often produce more sustainable outcomes than competition and hostility . Societies that foster collaboration , fairness , and social cohesion tend to thrive over longer periods . In this sense , peace is not merely a moral aspiration but a strategy aligned with human survival and flourishing . Yet if peace is beneficial , why is it so difficult to achieve ? One reason lies in the complexity of global systems . Nations operate within intricate networks of alliances , economic dependencies , historical grievances , and security concerns . Even when leaders desire peace , mistrust between rivals can create a security dilemma in which each side arms itself defensively , inadvertently escalating tensions . Additionally , unresolved historical wounds , whether territorial disputes , colonial legacies , or ethnic divisions can persist for generations , making reconciliation challenging . Another factor is the powerful influence of narratives and identities . Religion , ideology , and nationalism can inspire noble values , but they can also be manipulated to divide communities . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ than shared humanity , conflict becomes easier to justify . The challenge of the modern world is therefore not simply political but civilizational : humanity must learn to transcend divisive identities while respecting cultural diversity . Addressing these challenges requires innovative thinking that moves beyond traditional diplomatic approaches . One of the most powerful tools for long-term peace may be education . Imagine a global educational system that prioritizes emotional intelligence , ethical reasoning , environmental stewardship , and conflict resolution alongside mathematics and science . Children growing up with such education would be better equipped to understand different cultures , manage disagreements peacefully , and resist manipulation by divisive propaganda . Education that nurtures empathy and global citizenship could gradually transform the mindset of future generations . Another transformative idea involves leadership accountability . Throughout history , some philosophers have argued that political leaders who initiate wars should bear the same risks as those who fight them . While implementing such principles may be complex , the underlying concept is powerful : when decision-makers personally experience the consequences of their choices , they may approach conflict with greater caution @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in shaping global behaviour . Currently , vast resources are invested in military expenditure . If a portion of these funds were redirected toward collaborative global projects , such as climate action , renewable energy , public health , and poverty alleviation-nations might discover that cooperation yields greater benefits than confrontation . Shared challenges like climate change , pandemics , and environmental degradation transcend national boundaries . They remind us that humanity ultimately inhabits one fragile planet whose well-being depends on collective stewardship . Technological innovation may also contribute to peace if guided by ethical principles . Artificial intelligence , data analysis , and early warning systems could help identify potential conflicts before they escalate , enabling diplomatic intervention . At the same time , international cooperation will be essential to ensure that emerging technologies are not misused for surveillance , manipulation , or autonomous warfare . The ethical governance of technology may become one of the defining challenges of our era . However , beyond policies and institutions lies a deeper transformation that humanity must undergo : a shift in consciousness . Wars often arise from collective expressions of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ self-awareness , compassion , and humility , these destructive forces can gradually diminish . Spiritual traditions across cultures emphasize practices such as meditation , reflection , service , and gratitude as means to nurture inner peace . When individuals experience inner harmony , they are less likely to seek dominance over others . This transformation is not merely idealistic . History shows that profound social change often begins with shifts in collective values . The abolition of slavery , the expansion of human rights , and the global recognition of environmental responsibility all emerged from evolving moral awareness . Similarly , a future civilization that values empathy , sustainability , and cooperation over domination may eventually redefine the meaning of power itself . Imagine a world where nations compete not in accumulating weapons but in advancing knowledge , healing ecosystems , and improving human well-being . Imagine global recognition that the health of one region affects the stability of all others , just as organs within a body depend on each other . Such a vision may seem distant , yet many initiatives already move in this direction-international scientific collaborations @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ networks that transcend borders .
